I’m a fellow Canadian (Newfoundlander to be precise) who’s been reading your blog from the very beginning. Mostly it’s a case of “preaching to the converted”.

I’ve been spending winters in Arizona for the last 10 years because my partner (also from Newfoundland) lives in Chandler. And literally, no joke, the first item that I have written down on my list of things to do in Arizona this coming winter is “go check out Cul De Sac”.

Maybe if I go and wander around there, I’ll spot your facial hair

I don’t know if it’s weird to say this, but I’d be up for a coffee or a bike ride or some hang time or whatever if you feel so inclined. It would definitely be the weirdest way that I’ve ever made a friend. In a good way.

Anyway, obviously the desert has lots of beautiful hikes and bike rides. But do yourself a favour (note the “u” in favour LoL) and go check out The Desert Botanical Gardens. It’s one of the absolute gems in The Valley. It can sometimes have lots of tourists there … particularly us Canucks. But it’s for good reason. It is spectacular. And they have lots of cool events there too. We take all our visitors there. And if you’re so inclined, the library offers free passes to DBG and lots of other local attractions too.

(1) The Musical Instrument Museum is pretty huge and unique

(2) The drive out to Tortilla Flats is really beautiful. It literally is an old stage coach trail that was turned into a twisty 2 lane highway.  And you can go boating or kayaking in Canyon lake, which is pretty sweet.

(3) Sedona is obviously one of the most gorgeous places in the US and a reasonably short drive. If you’re going to go to the Grand Canyon from Sedona (or even if you’re just going to Flagstaff), there’s this fabulous older highway called 89A that takes you to Flagstaff. It’s so much more fun than taking the freeway.

(4) There are oodles and oodles of free Disc Golf courses (my new obsession and the price is right)

(5) South Mountain has a thing called “Silent Sunday” where they close the mountain to cars. So you can ride your bike up (obviously challenging) but then down (woo hoo!)

(6) There’s a cool thing downtown called “First Friday Art Walk” every month. Google it.

(7) Most importantly, my favourite place to ride my bike is in the Northern part of The McDowell Sonoran Preserve. Specifically, I like the trail called “The Long Way Around”. It’s just the right length (around 25 km). The ground is very beginner friendly. In fact, I have a hybrid, not a mountain bike and it does fine. But the trail still has lots of ups and downs and twists and turns, so it’s a blast. So much so, that the first time I rode there, I was giggling like a kid, even though I’m 55. It’s as easy or hard as you want it to be, based on how fast you go. And also it’s one of the nicest parks in the area.

(8) Taliesin West is super cool. Particularly if you get a good guide. It was Frank Lloyd Wright’s personal project. His winter home. So he was free to do whatever crazy things he could dream up, without having to account to a client. The handyman in you will love it!

I could go on, but that’s off the top of my head.

One last note. If you wear something Canadian; like for example, I wear a CBC logo on my hat or my partner wears something from the Leafs … a zillion snowbird Canadians will approach you and ask what part of Canada you’re from.

Anyway, here’s to a great time in Arizona.

Repeated or prolonged spinal flexion can increase stress on the tissues around the spine. The Jefferson curl targets spinal flexion by improving spinal control and strengthening positions you might find yourself in and out of the gym.

It’s considered an obscure exercise. If you’ve never heard of or seen it, you might think it’s the latest move for giving your biceps a pump. But the Jefferson curl is far from an arm-day exercise.

The Jefferson curl ia actually lower-back move—one that contradicts almost everything known about lower-back health. To perform it, you hold a weight in front of you and slowly lower it toward the floor while flexing your spine. In other words, you round your back under load and keep bending.

End-range spinal flexion is a key reason many trainers hesitate to add the Jefferson curl to their clients’ workouts. But for the right lifter, it can mean better control, greater flexion tolerance, and improved mobility. However, if it isn’t a good fit, it can increase your injury risk.

So, should you include it in your program?

According to two strength experts, the answer is, it depends.

The Jefferson curl is a controlled exercise where you deliberately flex the spine one segment at a time while holding a light weight. From the neck down, slowly round your back through the upper, middle, and lower back as you reach toward the floor.

The goal is not to see how far you can flex, but to control spinal flexion through a range you can own while placing the entire posterior-chain tissues under tension.

Sets and reps: According to Physical Therapist Bo Babenko, start with 3 to 5 repetitions at a time, using only 15 to 20 pounds as a stretch. Emphasize taking 2 to 3 deep breaths at the bottom, with an elongated exhale to stretch the tissues involved.

Placement: After your main strength work or during a mobility session.

The Jefferson curl challenges (arguably) one of strength training’s biggest blind spots: the idea that the spine should always stay rigid. Outside of a neutral spine while lifting, your spine is designed to move. You flex to tie your shoes, pick things up, sit, reach, climb, and perform plenty of athletic movements. Avoiding spinal flexion doesn’t prepare you for those demands.

That is where the Jefferson Curl can help. When performed well, it lets you train spinal flexion rather than encountering it when fatigued or in a variable environment. The point is not to teach you to round your back during a max deadlift. The point is to recognize that spinal stiffness and spinal movement are both movement skills.

But spinal flexion is dose-dependent. Too much of anything, even water, will hurt you.

That is why this lift deserves neither a blanket ban nor a free pass.

There are some rewards with the risk, and here they are.

One of its biggest benefits is that it asks you to move the spine one segment at a time, rather than treating your entire spine as a single rigid block. That controlled flexion and extension can improve body awareness and give you more options for how you move.

The Jefferson curl also places the hamstrings, spinal erectors, and other posterior tissues under tension through a longer ROM than many strength exercises. “I believe the Jefferson curl certainly has a place,” explains Babenko. “To decompress the spine and stretch out the posterior chain.”

Most flexibility work is passive, but the Jefferson curl takes a different approach by loading the range you are trying to improve. That means the hamstrings and trunk are not just becoming more flexible; they are learning to produce and control force in that range.

If your hamstrings are tight, your spinal control disappears, or you start chasing depth without control, you’ll find out quickly. That makes the exercise useful for both mobility assessment and training.

Repeated or prolonged spinal flexion can increase creep in passive tissues such as ligaments and discs, raising the risk of lower back injury. Critics view it as an unnecessary risk. Their argument is simple: if you can improve mobility without loading end-range spinal flexion, why take the chance?

Any lifter worth their salt knows to keep their back neutral during deadlifts, squats, and rows. “Most lifters need to generate, transfer, and resist substantial forces while maintaining core stiffness and controlling spinal motion,” explains strength coach Matt Wenning. “These exercises can develop these qualities without requiring loaded end-range spinal flexion.”

Loading flexion can blur the line between a controlled mobility drill and poor technique during heavy lifting.

It’s not meant as a strength test, but some people will always try to see how much weight they can do. “I had a patient show up with back pain,” says Babenko. “She was trying to build up well over 150 pounds on the Jefferson curl, and, well, she hurt her lower back.”

Too much load increases the risk. Instead of slow, controlled segmental flexion, you get a loaded collapse with little benefit.

Hamstring stretching, hip-hinge drills, and RDLs can all enhance hamstring mobility without taking the spine through deliberate loaded flexion. That makes the Jefferson Curl optional.

There is no direct research on the Jefferson curl itself—a point backed up by Wenning.

“Direct evidence that Jefferson curls improve athletic performance, prevent low-back injuries, or outperform established strength and mobility interventions is insufficient.”

But most research focuses on spinal flexion, segmental spinal movement, flexibility training, and how spinal tissues behave under repeated or prolonged flexion.

A 2023 study comparing spinal flexion and extension exercises with more trunk movement found improvements in spinal flexibility, including finger-to-floor distance. This supports one of the Jefferson curl’s main purposes: learning to move through spinal flexion gradually rather than treating the spine as a single rigid unit.

One study found that 20 minutes of full lumbar flexion altered passive tissue contributions and increased demand on the spinal extensors afterward, meaning the extensors had to work harder after sustained flexion.

That study focused on sustained or repeated flexion exposures, not a few slow Jefferson curls. A set of five deliberate reps is not the same dose as sitting or hanging in deep flexion for 20 minutes.

No current research says spinal flexion is dangerous. “The spine can certainly flex, and spinal flexion itself is not inherently dangerous,” says Wenning

You know the pros and cons, but that doesn’t determine whether the Jefferson curl is a good fit. But this does.

The Jefferson curl sits in the moderate- high risk, moderate-reward category. The risk comes from loaded spinal flexion. That does not mean flexion is dangerous, but it does mean the dose matters. Too much load, range, fatigue, or volume can turn this mobility drill into unnecessary stress on the spine’s passive tissues.

“Jefferson curls offer limited advantages for most lifters,” says Wenning. “Particularly when more established exercises can address the same training goals with greater specificity and more controllable loading.”

The reward is that the Jefferson curl can train something most strength programs avoid: controlled spinal flexion. It can improve segmental spinal control, reveal mobility restrictions, and load the posterior chain through a long range of motion. For healthy lifters who tolerate flexion well, it can be useful.

The biggest factor in the risk-to-reward equation is intent. If you treat the Jefferson curl like a max-strength lift, the risk climbs fast. If you treat it like a light, slow, carefully progressed mobility-strength drill, the equation changes.

The reward isn’t massive, and the risk isn’t trivial, which is why this exercise belongs in the “use with a reason” category rather than the “everyone should do it” one.

The Jefferson curl isn’t one-size-fits-all, and people have opinions on both sides of the spectrum. Critics see a rounded spine and assume danger. Supporters sometimes swing too far the other way and act like controlled flexion makes the spine bulletproof.

Many exercises have a larger margin for error, like biceps curls, while others have a smaller margin, like the Jefferson curl. That means you should approach this exercise with caution.

But for the right lifter, used with light loads and a slow progression, it can be one way to train a position most strength programs avoid altogether. Spinal flexion sometimes happens, so it helps to be prepared.

The problem isn’t always spinal flexion; it’s treating flexion without respect.

#8628. The Best Smith Machine for Your Home Gym in 2025

The Smith machine sometimes gets a bad rap, but it can be a solid addition to any home gym.

Written by Stephen Sheehan, CPT × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC Last updated on Nov 2, 2026

expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC

Other than the almighty treadmill, there may not be a piece of equipment more synonymous with commercial gyms than the Smith machine. Boasting tremendous versatility and functionality, this muscle-building tool is popular among lifters of all experience levels.

However, you don’t need a gym membership to enjoy its benefits. While it may have not been a home gym staple years ago, the Smith machine has become a must-have for many fitness enthusiasts. Offering added protection without a spotter for your bench presses, back squats, deadlifts, and other strength exercises, the Smith machine is a wise investment for those trying to build the ultimate garage gym.

With options spanning from traditional Smith machines to all-in-one home gym solutions, you might feel a bit overwhelmed about which direction to go. Luckily for you, our team of expert product testers did all the due diligence necessary to separate the cream from the crop. From analyzing the build materials to testing the smoothness of the bar path to assessing the value, we took the time to dissect each element in order to narrow down our list to just five.

In addition, we got some valuable insight from Mauro S. Maietta, district fitness and education manager for Crunch Fitness, on the benefits and what factors to consider when you’re shopping for a Smith machine.

This content is meant to be informative, but should not be taken as medical advice. It is not intended for use as diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of health problems. Always speak with your doctor before starting any new supplement or exercise regimen.

If you’re searching for a multifunctional Smith machine that’s compatible with a ton of attachments, the Force USA G15 is the machine that can truly do it all — albeit at an expensive price point of around $5,500. However, there’s a reason it earned 4.5 out of 5 stars for versatility from our top product tester: you can perform a wide variety of exercises by taking advantage of all of its functionality.

Tipping the scales at nearly 1,000 pounds, the G15 combines a functional trainer, half rack, and Smith machine into a single, sturdy unit. Measuring over 6 feet wide, over 4 feet deep, and about 7 feet tall, the G15 earns a 4-star footprint rating. While there are more compact options, it’s still a good option for folks with limited space, especially considering the versatility you get.

Offering dual 289-pound weight stacks that keep it well-anchored, the G15 also scores 4 out of 5 stars for durability and construction.

“This thing is like a tank,” our tester says. “Once it’s assembled, it’ll basically be stuck in place.”

Unfortunately, our tester wasn’t as impressed with the cable pulley material. Asthey’re made from nylon instead of aluminum, they don’t move as smoothly and won’t be as durable as their metal counterparts.

Something that separates the G15 from many competitors is its ability to go from a 2:1 or 4:1 pulley ratio. This gives you the ability to make the weight feel like half or a quarter of the actual weight. While our tester would prefer a 1:1 ratio for more effective resistance, he says the 2:1 or 4:1 ratios “will be adequate for most people working out from home.”

The G15 comes with a lengthy list of attachments, including J-hooks, safety spotter arms, multi-grip dip handles, a multi-grip pull-up bar, band pegs, and a low row footplate. If you want to unlock even more training possibilities, the $700 G15 Upgrade Kit includes three additional strength training stations, three functional attachments, a TV mount, and four storage shelves.

Two knocks against this ultra-versatile machine: assembly and value.

Although some of the parts arrive pre-assembled, our assembly expert recommends budgeting “at least 20 man hours” to get the G15 fully put together. And if you want to leave it to the professionals, you’ll need to pay an additional $800.

At nearly $6,000 on its own, the G15 certainly isn’t made for budget-conscious shoppers. Our top product tester gave it 3.5 out of 5 stars for value, noting that Force USA could use better quality components, cables, and accessories, including one of the key parts of this premium-priced unit: the built-in barbell.“The knurling is super passive and not going to allow for an adequate grip for the user if you were to go heavy on any Smith machine movements,” he explains.

Want to crush a full-body workout with a single piece of equipment? The Titan Fitness Smith Machine can be the all-in-one solution that allows you to train your upper body, lower body, and core in a safe, effective manner.

Is it as versatile as the G15? No. Is it far more affordable? Yes.

For less than a third of the price, you can still get an excellent workout experience from the $1,7000 Titan Smith Machine. One of our more seasoned product testers used it for a variety of strength training sessions, highlighting how impressed she was by the smooth glide of the barbell and the angled design. In addition, this Smith machine is counterbalanced so you don’t have to support the entire 45-pound barbell like you do on other machines. Beginners will appreciate this, as the bar only feels like 15 pounds.

Unfortunately, like Force USA, Titan left our team wanting more out of the knurling.

“It’s fine for a Smith machine, but it’s definitely not the most grippy bar,” our tester says.

On the other hand, this machine earns high marks for its ergonomics. Our tester rated it 4 out of 5 stars in this category. She found the single-axis, angled design helped improve her muscle activation during lower-body weight training exercises like Smith machine squats and lunges.

Most importantly, she felt completely secure using this Titan machine. Not only was there no wobbling or shaking, but the bar moved smoothly, leading her to give a 5-out-of-5 rating for stability.

“This is a super stable machine; there was no give to it even when we were using heavy weights,” our tester says. “This was ultra-smooth.” While Titan priced this machine fairly, we’d like to see a better warranty. A one-year policy falls well short of what we expect from most brands. Plus, if you want to return a piece of equipment, you must pay the return shipping costs and a 20% restocking fee. That results in a disappointing customer experience score of just 2 out of 5 stars.

Don’t want a standalone Smith machine? Bolt Fitness has a space-saving solution in the form of the Storm Series Stinger Smith Machine Attachment. Compatible with any 3” x 3” frame using 1” hardware, this universal attachment can seamlessly integrate with your existing squat or power rack, opening the door to even more training possibilities.

We rate this Smith machine attachment a 4.5 out of 5 for versatility, as it offers 12 different positions totaling 60” of vertical adjustments. That means you can quickly go from a steep incline bench press to a Romanian deadlift, making your workouts more efficient, too. Plus, we also like that this attachment has a 43” built-in multi-grip pull-up bar, giving you the ability to develop your vertical pulling strength and endurance.

Bolt also earns solid marks for construction, earning 4 out of 5 stars in this key category. However, our chief product tester warns not to expect quite the same level of craftsmanship as some better-known brands.

“You won’t see the same quality welds or powder coats from Bolt as you will from Rogue or REP,” he says.

Like several other nominees on this list, our tester was also disappointed with the Smith bar’s knurling. The passive knurl pattern won’t give you a particularly stable grip, especially when using heavier weights.

“You definitely won’t mistake this for an Olympic barbell,” our tester says.

As for the price? At around $1,100 this is on the expensive side for a Smith machine attachment. For example, the Bells of Steel Smith Machine Rack Attachment is much more affordable at $800. We rate it a 3 out of 5 for value, especially since you already need a rack to use it. Otherwise, expect to invest a significant chunk of change to get a fully functioning setup.

Just because you can’t afford to splurge on something like the G15 doesn’t mean you can’t find a Smith machine that fits within your budget. If you don’t have a ton of financial wiggle room, the RitFit Smith Machine is the most affordable option that earned our stamp of approval.

As our top product tester puts it, “If you’re looking for a Smith machine and you’re on an ultra-budget, this is it.”

At about $500 on Amazon, this machine is less than a third of the price of the Titan Fitness Smith Machine and less than a tenth of the cost of the G15. Of course, it’s not the most durable option on the market, but it offers sufficient versatility at a very attractive price point to earn a near-perfect value rating of 4.5 out of 5 stars.

Dubbed the “sleeper pick” by our tester, he notes that “the low price covers so many sins.”

Before we dive into some of RitFit’s shortcomings, let’s highlight some of the strengths of this machine. First, we rated it 4 out of 5 for versatility, as it offers built-in low row and lat pulldown capabilities using a plate-loaded cable pulley system that holds 165 pounds. The RitFit Smith Machine also comes with several attachments, including a pin-on landmine row and two multi-purpose pull-up handles.

Secondly, it has a compact design that makes it suitable for home gym setups with limited  space. It also weighs just 140 pounds, making it easier to move than other options on this list.

However, our tester had several callouts about the RitFit Smith Machine that deserve mentioning. With cheaper build materials and a lightweight design, it didn’t prove to be as stable as he would have liked, earning just 3.5 out of 5 stars for both construction and stability. Needless to say, this isn’t the best option if you want to lift heavy weights. Still, considering you could pay around the same price for a high-quality Olympic barbell, the RitFit Smith Machine is a solid option if you’re on a limited budget.

Imagine if you could turn your squat rack into a Smith machine in a matter of minutes. That dream can be a reality if you’re willing to invest around $700 on the VTS Lite Rack Attachment from Bulletproof Fitness, a lesser-known fitness equipment manufacturer that’s caught our attention.

While we haven’t gotten our hands on this attachment just yet, it’s hard not to get excited about the concept and execution by Bulletproof. The Versa Trolley System (VTS) Lite allows you to convert your squat rack into a Smith machine using your own barbell. The rollers are made from UHMW plastic, an ultra-durable material we’ve seen used on other racks. This attachment only weighs 15 pounds, making the VHS Lite a more user-friendly alternative than the full-sized VTS, which weighs in at 24 pounds. From a construction standpoint, we feel comfortable giving the VTS Lite 4 out of 5 stars.

In addition, we like that Bulletproof offers a wide range of options to accommodate different racks. You can choose between a 3” x 3” pair, a 2” x 3” pair, or a 2” x 2” pair. You also can choose different hook sizes based on the diameter of your barbell. This optionality, along with the added exercise variety you get from using the attachments, earns a 4.5 out of 5 for versatility.

Set to be released in May 2025, we’re excited to see this product in action. If you want a more streamlined solution than getting a standalone Smith machine, this is an attractive space- and money-saving solution. Based on the price and versatility, we give it a value rating of 4 out of 5 — though it could go higher once we get our hands on it.

As Smith machines have become more popular among the home gym community, we’ve ramped up our efforts to test ones from a variety of brands. This has allowed us to develop a thorough evaluation process that examines a number of key factors that impact your workout experience.

With options ranging from standard Smith machines to all-in-one trainers with cable machines, here’s what we assess during testing using a 1-5 scoring system:

What makes a Smith machine such a valuable training tool? If you’ve ever used one, you already know there’s added peace of mind knowing you have built-in support. Here’s an overview of the different benefits of utilizing this popular piece of equipment.

Unlike when you use a barbell and squat rack, the Smith machine provides a fixed bar path. This can help reduce the risk of injury and ensure a stable lifting environment.

“The Smith machine helps the athlete feel supported and gives them greater control and stability when performing an exercise,” says Mauro M. Maietta, district fitness and education manager for Crunch Fitness.

In particular, new lifters can benefit from starting out on a Smith machine so they can focus on their form while being supported by the machine.

“Maintaining correct form is important for avoiding injuries and maximizing the effectiveness of your workouts,” says Dr. Christopher Mohr, PhD, RD. “Beginners might benefit from working with a personal trainer initially or taking a beginner class to learn proper techniques.”

The guided motion and added stability of a Smith machine makes it an ideal training tool for those returning from injury or anyone with mobility issues. It encourages proper form and can be a safer way to increase your strength and joint stability before moving on to free weights.

Maietta recommends starting with lighter weights to get a feel for the range of motion before progressing. “The fixed range of motion is not for everyone, so be sure to speak with your local fitness professional and listen to your body and joints if you feel any discomfort or pain during the planned movements,” he says.

If you prefer to work out alone or don’t have a training partner available, the Smith machine can act as a “spotter” for you. These machines offer an extra layer of safety, as you can easily rack the bar or set the safety spotters to a specific point that will keep you out of harm’s way.

In addition, this advantage allows you to safely follow progressive overload, a proven method for increasing muscle size and strength.

“This continual challenge helps your muscles grow stronger,” says Mohr. “It’s important to start with manageable increments to prevent injury.”

You won’t find many machines that offer as much versatility as the Smith machine. Want to train legs? You can knock out squat and lunge variations. Want to grow your chest and shoulders? Grab an adjustable weight bench and work on your bench press and overhead press without having to worry about keeping the bar stable. A high-end option like the Force USA G15 gives you the ability to perform cable exercises like cable crossovers, chest flys, and overhead triceps extensions.

“The Smith machine can be seen as the Swiss army knife of the weight room since it allows for several strength training exercises in its fixed vertical path, ranging from squats to overhead pressing movements,” says Maietta.

What should you consider when choosing a Smith machine? Based on our experience as equipment experts and dedicated lifters, here’s what we recommend:

Consider the machine’s footprint when determining if it is a good fit for your needs. One benefit of Smith machines is all-in-one trainers are available to consolidate the space needed for multiple workout stations.

Many of the home gym Smith machine options on this list are designed as all-in-one trainers designed to provide multiple workout functions with one convenient machine. The machine can include stations for a power rack, functional trainer, low-row attachment, chin-ups/pull-ups, dips, suspension trainers, and more.

Smith machines offer pulley systems with varying weight ratios, including 1:1 and 2:1. A 1:1 ratio means the weight you load is the exact weight you lift. A 2:1 ratio means you lift half of the weight you load. For instance, with a 2:1 ratio, if you load 100 pounds, you lift 50 pounds.

Some Force USA Smith machines, including the G15, allow users to easily switch between 2:1 and 4:1 ratios, which is helpful when people of various skills use the same machine.

Weight capacities vary depending on the functions offered by the machine. The weight capacities on this list start at 300 pounds. Be sure to confirm the machine’s weight capacity can accommodate your needs..

If you are looking for versatile strength-building home gym equipment to achieve a full-body workout, a Smith machine can help you achieve your goals. Since the 1950s, this game-changing machine has allowed gym-goers to work out safely without a spotter. Today, there is a wide range of consumer options, allowing you to experience the benefits of the Smith machine in the comfort of your own home gym.

Smith machines all perform similar functions, but there are different types of Smith machines available. For instance, some Smith machines provide a vertical path for motion, while other Smith machines provide a slightly angled path. Some Smith machines may be limited to the Smith machine function, while others are designed to be all-in-one machines with multiple stations for different exercises. Smith machines vary based on the manufacturer.

Yes, you can deadlift on a Smith machine, but whether you should depends on your skills and ability.Maietta suggests thinking through the following questions before performing moves on a Smith machine:-How is your range of motion?-Do you have the proper form or mobility to perform these compound moves?If you do not know, Maietta suggests working with a local fitness professional who will be able to help coach you and correct your form if necessary.

Yes, you can build muscle with the consistent use of a Smith machine. Smith machines are considered a good strength and muscle training option for beginners or those without a spotter. However, the drawback is motion is limited to a specific vertical (or slightly angled) path. For sports-specific muscle building, some experts prefer free weight exercises.

Yes, you can squat with a Smith machine. Safety features such as hooks and stoppers can help provide extra protection. Again, be mindful of your abilities and consult with a fitness pro if you are unsure of how to do this safely and with proper form.

#8627. Scott Eastwood Is Still Seeking a Rush, Just at a Slower Pace

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

He still surfs. He still trains jiujitsu and Muay Thai. And the actor still lifts and still enjoys putting himself in situations that demand something from him physically.

What has changed at 40 is the way he prepares for all of it.

There was a time when Eastwood could train hard, wake up sore, and trust that his body would bounce back. Now, he is far more interested in staying mobile, pain-free, and ready for whatever he wants to do outside the gym.

Over the last five years, Eastwood says that shift has become increasingly intentional.

“Recovery is probably the biggest difference,” Eastwood told M&F. “I think I’d probably put it number one. I listen to my body more and take more care in my recovery than I ever did in my 20s or 30s.”

This doesn’t mean that he’s less serious about training, it just means Eastwood’s objective has evolved. Looking like a capable athlete has given way to a much more important goal: staying physically capable.

“Obviously I want to be strong, but I also want to be really flexible and limber and be able to react to whatever the world throws at you, where you’re not going to pull something or you’re not going to hurt yourself.”

Eastwood ,who’s latest film, Lucky Strike, is now streaming on Hulu, used to organize his gym work around the familiar bodybuilding split—chest, back, and different muscle groups on different days.

Now he prefers training that puts his entire body to work.

“I think [now I’m] just a little bit more focused on holistic workouts,” Eastwood said. “I’m far more focused now on my core, just because of body pain and how your body feels, and all the things that feel better, which kind of stem out from your core.”

When he isn’t working on a film, Eastwood says he typically lifts three or four times per week, splitting those sessions between gym and home workouts. He also tries to fit in Muay Thai or jiujitsu. Yoga has become a constant.

Eastwood says there isn’t a day that passes where he doesn’t do some version of it, often half an hour in the morning and another later in the day.

When he is filming, the expectations change.

A 6 a.m. call time might require a 5 a.m. gym session. Long production days can already be physically taxing, so those workouts become less about progress. It’s an evolution in the thinking that every training session needs to prove something. Eastwood still trains hard, but there isn’t much value now in forcing his body through movements that no longer feel worth the risk.

“You’re spending a lot of time on your feet, and it’s typically physical,” Eastwood said. “So you’re kind of just doing a little more maintenance when you’re working. You’re not getting the gains that you might get if you’re not working.”

The gym has never been the only testing grounds for Eastwood.

Surfing, martial arts, and hiking are still a part of his life, and each demands something slightly different from his body.

It’s a large part why strength alone no longer satisfies him.

“If I want to continue to do jiujitsu, and I want to do Muay Thai, and I want to continue to surf, I’ve got to take care of my body,” Eastwood says. “Which means strength, flexibility, and mobility. I’ve got to kind of do all these things, or my body is going to get trashed doing these sports.”

Those activities also provide him with feedback that a mirror will miss. A stiff body doesn’t perform well on a surfboard. Poor mobility isn’t less obvious when someone is trying to control you on a mat. Carrying unnecessary soreness into either activity can turn something meant to be enjoyable into a problem quickly.

Eastwood hasn’t lost his appetite for these passions that come with risk. However, age has made him more selective about which risks within those passions are worth taking.

That means foregoing chasing a massive surf or testing himself on the mat against whoever wants to go the hardest. When he was younger, these thoughts might have not even entered into his thinking.

Now, it’s more thoughtful. He still wants the challenge, to compete with himself, and to feel capable. These activities are just no longer a barometer for his toughness.

Ask him what physical quality matters more now than it did at 25, and the answer is an understandable one.

“Flexibility,” Eastwood says. “Flexibility and just not being in pain. If you can take care of your body where you’re not in pain all the time, that’s really valuable.”

One of the biggest shifts for Eastwood is the attention to recovery.

Yoga, sauna sessions, and Epsom salt baths have all been part of his routine for years, but sleep has become especially important as both his training and work demands have changed.

“Just getting a good night’s sleep, I value it so much more now,” Eastwood says.

10 to 15-hour set days require focus, energy, and often physical effort. Arriving not fully rested often produces immediate consequences.

“I can’t do the job that I do well and focus if I haven’t had a great night’s sleep,” he said.

His approach to nutrition is also uncomplicated. Eastwood says he follows a Mediterranean-style diet built around whole foods, including fish, red meat, grains, and plenty of vegetables. He also refuses to turn an occasional bag of chips or dessert into a moral crisis.

“I don’t make it some hard and fast rule that you have to do,” he says. “I just think those just get a little too rigid.”

His preference for simplicity also played a role in why Eastwood became a co-owner of North Performance.

Eastwood says longtime friend Mike Lucas shared the frustration of trying to travel while managing individual supplements. Both men wanted something easier to maintain without pretending a supplement could replace the fundamentals.

“You still have to work out. You have to get good sleep and have good recovery,” he says. “Having good supplements is just going to help those things. The basics are the basics. They don’t change regardless.”

When he is filming, Eastwood says North is part of his morning routine, but the rest of his priorities remain the same.

He still has to eat well. He still has to move. If the day is packed and there are only 25 minutes for himself, he’ll find somewhere to fit in exercise, yoga, or mobility work. Everything beyond that is what he calls “extra credit.”

It’s a simplicity that defines fitness at 40 for him.

Looking strong doesn’t mean anything if his back is aching or his body is too tight to do the things all of his training was meant to prepare him for.

The goal going into the next decade is simple: keep enough strength to be useful, maintain mobility to move well, and have enough durability to keep saying yes to the things he enjoys.

“I think fit is more how you feel and less aesthetic,” Eastwood said. “[Looking good] is great, but if you’re in pain because you’re not doing it correctly, then who gives a shit about what you look like?”

The only points path to nonstop business class service to French Polynesia

Picture this: you're reclining in a fully flat bed somewhere over the Pacific, a glass of Champagne in hand, watching the sun melt into the ocean from 35,000 feet. In eight hours, you'll land in Papeete — French Polynesia's gateway to overwater bungalows, turquoise lagoons, and the kind of trip people save their whole lives for. And you got here on points. This is the Air France business class seat to Tahiti, and it represents one of the most emotionally resonant redemptions in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. Not just because of where you're going — though Tahiti is bucket-list by definition — but because of the staggering gap between what you'd pay in cash and what you'll pay in miles. **The math will genuinely stop you in your tracks.** A business class ticket from Los Angeles (LAX) to Papeete (PPT) on Air France regularly retails between **$5,000 and $12,000 per person**. That's the cash reality. But with Flying Blue miles — Air France-KLM's frequent flyer program — you can book the same seat for as few as **88,000 miles**. At the high end of retail pricing, that's a value of **13.6 cents per point (CPP)**. Even at the low end, you're extracting **5.7 CPP** from miles that most programs value at 1–2 cents. In the ChooseFI community, we talk constantly about optimizing every dollar toward financial independence — and a redemption that turns 88,000 transferable points into a $5,000–$12,000 experience is about as powerful as it gets. Here's what makes this feel different from your average business class booking: Air France operates a **Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner** on this route, featuring a modern, premium business class cabin with direct aisle access for every seat, noise-reducing windows, better humidity levels, and that unmistakably French touch in service and catering. You're not just flying in a recliner — you're flying in a genuine lie-flat pod on one of aviation's most celebrated aircraft. And this is the only nonstop option. Air France is the **sole carrier operating nonstop LAX–PPT** service. That's not a coincidence — it's a pricing inefficiency baked into the route's geography, and it's exactly the kind of structural advantage the ChooseFI community knows how to exploit.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: Air France-KLM's Flying Blue program is the only way to book the only nonstop flight between Los Angeles and Tahiti using points — and that program happens to offer some of the most generous award pricing in the world.

Flying Blue uses a dynamic award pricing model, meaning costs fluctuate based on demand and availability. That sounds like a disadvantage — and sometimes it is. But here's the inefficiency: Flying Blue releases Promo Rewards every single month. These are fixed-price award seats on select routes, discounted 25–50% off standard award pricing. When Tahiti appears as a Promo Reward destination (which it does periodically), the pricing drops dramatically — and crucially, Promo Reward tickets eliminate carrier-imposed fuel surcharges entirely.

Fuel surcharges on Air France-operated flights are normally moderate, but they're real — they can add $200–$500 to an award ticket. Promo Rewards wipe those out. This is the pricing inefficiency: Flying Blue is essentially subsidizing this cabin to drive demand, and you can capture the subsidy.

Here's the beautiful part for ChooseFI members: virtually every major transferable points currency sends to Flying Blue at a 1:1 ratio. That means:

The Chase, Amex, and Citi transfers are instant, which matters enormously when you're racing to lock down a business class award seat before someone else grabs it. You find the seat, you confirm it's available, then you transfer — because once points leave your bank, they don't come back.

This is the single most important rule in booking award travel, and it's especially critical here. Flying Blue's award availability on the LAX–PPT route is genuinely limited — this is a popular route to a popular destination on a single aircraft. You do not transfer points speculatively. You find confirmed availability on flyingblue.com, verify the seat count and pricing, then immediately transfer from your Chase, Amex, or Citi account (all instant) and book.

Flying Blue allows open-jaw routing, meaning you could potentially fly into Papeete and out of another South Pacific destination if Air France serves it — giving sophisticated travelers a way to build a multi-destination itinerary without paying for a separate return trip to your origin city. It's a small but meaningful piece of flexibility in a program that doesn't always offer it.

This is a moderate-difficulty booking. The steps themselves aren't complicated — but the sequencing matters enormously. Follow this in order.

Go to flyingblue.com and use the award search tool. You do NOT need a Flying Blue account to search — but you will need one to book, so create a free account if you haven't already. Search LAX → PPT in business class. Flying Blue's calendar view lets you scan across multiple departure dates, which is essential for spotting availability on a route with limited award seats.

Tip: Flying Blue's booking window opens 359 days in advance. For a route this popular and this capacity-constrained, searching at the 11-month mark is strongly advised. Set a calendar reminder for exactly 359 days before your target travel dates.

On the first of each month, Flying Blue releases its new Promo Rewards. These are fixed-price, reduced-cost awards with no fuel surcharges. Bookmark flyingblue.com/en/earn-spend/flying-blue-promo-rewards and check it monthly. If Tahiti appears, act immediately — Promo Reward availability disappears fast.

Once you find available dates and seats, note the exact miles price shown at checkout. Flying Blue's dynamic pricing means the cost you see on Monday might differ from Thursday. Screenshot the search result with the price clearly visible. This is your confirmation that the award is priceable before you transfer points.

Now — and only now — transfer your points:

Transfer the exact amount you need — no more, no less.

Return to flyingblue.com, complete the search again with your now-funded account, and book. Have your passport and traveler details ready. Pay any taxes/fees (usually $50–$150 on non-Promo awards; near-zero on Promo Rewards) with a travel rewards credit card to earn additional points.

Award availability on this route moves quickly. If your target dates are sold out:

Flying Blue uses dynamic award pricing, which usually makes award charts unpredictable. When Tahiti appears on the Promo Rewards list, business class pricing drops 25 to 50 percent below standard and fuel surcharges are eliminated entirely. Air France is the sole operator of the LAX to PPT nonstop — no other airline flies it — which means Flying Blue is the only loyalty program with direct booking access to this route. This combination of route exclusivity and periodic promotional pricing is what makes this a genuine sweet spot rather than just a good redemption.

Let's make this concrete. Imagine a couple planning their 10th anniversary trip to Bora Bora in the spring of 2026. They want to start the trip right — meaning lie-flat seats over the Pacific, not a middle seat in economy for a nine-hour flight.

The points price: 88,000 Flying Blue miles per person, round-trip in business class. For two passengers: 176,000 Flying Blue miles total, plus approximately $200–$300 in taxes and carrier fees (less if you catch a Promo Rewards release, where surcharges are waived entirely).

The CPP math: At $8,000 in cash value against 88,000 miles, you're extracting 9.1 cents per point — nearly 5–9x the baseline value of transferable points currencies. That's the ChooseFI lens: every point you've earned on everyday spending just multiplied in purchasing power.

What you'll actually experience: You check in at LAX and are directed to the business class line — a detail that still feels quietly luxurious no matter how many times you've done it. Once onboard the Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner, your seat converts to a fully flat bed of approximately 6 feet in length. Air France's catering reflects its French heritage: expect a proper multi-course meal service, a curated wine selection, and warm bread — not a foil-wrapped tray. The flight is roughly 8–9 hours nonstop, so there's time to genuinely sleep, watch a film, and arrive rested.

For a couple using points they accumulated from normal household spending over 12–18 months, the $16,000 in combined cash value they didn't spend is the real number — and the one that matters most on the path to FI.

#8624. Science Finds that Dairy May Not Lead to Excess Fat as First Thought

For a long time, the public were cautioned against regular dairy food consumption, but a recent study from the University of Toronto, published by the Journal of Nutrition, appears to show that frequently delving into eggs, milk, and cheeses, could actually benefit your health and won’t make you fat. Here’s why.

In the ‘70s, a war on saturated fat consumption encouraged us to avoid products like whole milk, butter, and cheese because of the high levels that they contain. Then wellness culture in the new millennium further derailed the case for diary, citing inflammation, acne, and disrupted hormones on this food stuff. Of course, some people are lactose intolerant, and have problems processing dairy food, but the Toronto study has challenged the campaign against dairy, with some surprisingly edible results.

74 overweight adults undertook a 12-week study and were randomly assigned to one of three groups:

All the groups were counseled on healthy eating, so that they could manage their food intake. At the completion of the trial, the team took measurements including body weight, composition, cholesterol, blood markers, and metabolic health.

In both of the regular high fat dairy eating groups, the participants experienced improvements in their blood pressure while consuming a greater amount of protein, calcium, and vitamin D than the first group. Importantly, neither their waistlines nor BMI suffered. “Those that had three servings of dairy didn’t have adverse levels of blood cholesterol or lipids or evidence of insulin resistance,” explained Gerald Harvey Anderson, who was the lead author and works in the Faculty of Medicine at the University of Toronto.”

With full-fat dairy containing more saturated fat than reduced fat products, how could this be? The experts believe that dairy’s combination of fats and protein is what makes it a positive food. “With dairy products, it’s got two proteins, casein and whey, that are bound together with fat and with nutrients mixed in,” said Anderson. The “Dairy Matrix Hypothesis” suggests that the physical structure of dairy determines how the body processes its nutrient profile.

Of course, ice cream, milkshakes, and other treats that contain a ton saturated fat as well as massive amounts of sugar is a different story, but the Toronto study said its results with natural dairy products showed that  “Neither treatment nor time affected waist circumference, fat and fat-free mass, resting metabolic rate, fasting blood cholesterol, and urine creatinine.” The team concluded that “Frequent and daily consumption of full-fat dairy as part of a healthy diet is consistent with CFG (Canada’s Food Guide).”

This news also adds to another promising benefit of dairy, that was reported earlier this year. The American Academy of Neurology showed that those who regularly ate high fat cheese presented a 13% lower risk of dementia overall, and a 29% risk of vascular dementia. Cream was also associated with a 16% lower risk of all-type dementias.

The Toronto study found dairy to be a significant source of magnesium and potassium to boot. “The results align with the conclusion of an expert group that there is no evidence to support the avoidance of high-fat dairy in diets,” it said.

#8621. How to Correctly Add Forward and Reverse Lunges into Your Legday Workouts

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

When it comes to strengthening your legs, building muscles in your lower body, and improving all-round balance, lunges are a great move to lean into, but what is the difference between the forward and backward lunge? In a recent Instagram post, IFBB Pro, endurance athlete, and transformation coach Petar Klancir demonstrated the details.

Take a step in the right direction with these unique lunges.

“What is the difference?” asked The Croatian Colossus, who has built an Instagram base of more than one million followers thanks to his informative training videos. In essence, both of these variations are compound movements, so they tax multiple muscle groups at the same time. Whether you lunge forward or backward, you’ll be working the quads, hamstrings, calves and core. You will also flex the hips either way. But what does change is the emphasis placed on each muscle, and how they build your legs in different ways, as Klancir showed.

“Front step lunges target the quads more, due to the mechanics of the exercise,” explained Klancir. “The emphasis is on stepping forward, which requires the quads to control the impact of the foot’s landing. And there is a high degree of flexion.”

The quads take the majority of the load with forward lunges, because the mechanics that Klancir mentioned, require the quads to negotiate the lowering, and then lift your center of mass and return you to the starting position.

Tip: To avoid knee stress, be sure not to step out too far forward on the lunge. At the bottom of the lunge, your knee should only just be ahead of your chin.

“Back step lunges target the glutes and hamstrings,” said Klancir. “Due to emphasized hip-hinge movement.”

Reverse lunges are often considered easier to execute, because the front foot remains flat on the floor, providing a greater foundation and less requirement for core balance. They are also less stressful on the knee, because the load is shifted by the hamstrings and glutes to a greater extent than the quads.

Tip: Keep the front foot stable by keeping knee over ankle at all times.

For a complete leg blaster, your can try both movements by focusing on form. Then, once you are comfortable with your foot placings, you can build in some additional hypertrophy by adding a pair of dumbbells to the overall load.

#8619. How Rucking Helped ‘Outlander’ Star Sam Retford Become Battle Ready

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Sam Retford, who is known to millions of Outlander: Blood of my Blood fans as Dougal MacKenzie, looks very comfortable on a show that requires him to navigate the unpredictable Scottish terrain, and there’s a good reason why. Not only does Retford love the great outdoors, but he’s also vastly experienced in a variety of skills. From riding a horse to cave diving, or rucking to offroad bike racing, this actor is as able as they come. So, staying still for just a second, Retford tells M&F why Outlander is such a personal and professional high, and how his favorite pastimes informed the role and his physique.

Now living in Glasgow, Retford’s love of adventure was passed down through blood. “My mum was a proper ranch cowgirl,” says Retford, who was born in Australia. “She has ridden horses all around the world, so she taught me to ride.” The star says that he loves nothing more than to get a bunch of pals together and go exploring, and has recently biked in The Himalayas, crossed the rivers of Amazonia, and cave dived around the United Kingdom. When the news came down that Retford would take up the role of Dougal MacKenzie and battle it out in 18th century Scotland, he was understandably all-in.

While most actors stay within the confines of a gym to ready for their roles, Retford added to his indoor workouts by acclimatizing to his new filming environment. As War Chieftain Dougal MacKenzie, Retford wanted to get a feel for the rugged highland landscape. “I wanted this guy to be physically capable,” he tells M&F, noting that he practiced rucking up and down the hills with a weighted backpack. “Even going and sleeping in the heather. I really wanted to build a physique capable of doing these long winter treks, but remain flexible enough to be agile in battle, to be strong enough to carry heavy loads—so everything had to be functional.”

The type of physique required to hunt and survive in the wilds of Scotland would not require a six-pack or be akin to an underwear model, so Retford wanted to build his character with authenticity. “I wanted him to have a big strong back and strong legs,” says the actor. “Okay, he can, lift but can he swing a sword around as well?”

Sam Retford earned a second-degree black belt in Taekwondo in his youth and understands the importance of exercise for agility and injury prevention. He also likes to swing the Indian Mace Bells for balance. But in the gym, his workouts include plyometric moves that require explosive power, such as box jumps. When lifting weights, the star focuses on time under tension and replicating proper form while squatting or making an overhead press.

The star also introduced instability into his lifting elements, for example with elevated platforms or unilateral movements in order to prepare him for the uneven ground outside. Still, the actor says that ultimately, the best way to prepare for his sprinting and fighting scenes was to run in the woods and climb trees. “Just moving about on set and staying warm,” he recalls.

Fans of Outlander: Blood of My Blood will have noticed that the physicality has leveled up in Season 2. For example, Dougal MacKenzie becomes embroiled in a serious battle in Episode 5 and must be rescued from being trapped underwater in Episode 6. Fortunately, the enthusiastic adventurer is more than comfortable with holding his breath. In Episode 2, Dougal also found himself in a fistfight with Brian Fraser (played by Jamie Roy).

Retford wants people to know, however, that progress is individual, takes time, and is not as easy as some social media accounts would like you to believe. He is also keen to point out that it takes a team of stunt coordinators, special effects wizards, lighting, and audio technicians to make any actor appear at their best. “You’ll notice I do quite a lot of shield work and headbutting, as opposed to sword fighting,” he explains. “That’s because I’m a lefty, and my right-handed combat is not very good. So, I have to keep the sword well and truly sheathed for a lot of it, to not cut anyone’s fingers off!”

Blood of My Blood no doubt the dream job for this thrill seeker. “Just to be out there in the cold, in the thick of it, running around, swinging swords. I mean, it’s a beautiful type of physicality, and it’s an amazing thing to call your job. So, I try never to complain. I’m always grateful.”

With Retford more than open to battling through a third season of Outlander: Blood of My Blood, the talented performer is also producing an upcoming documentary in Uganda and also has an eye on traveling to Mexico. “The key is to just say yes to crazy things,” he beams.

Season 2 of Outlander: Blood of My Blood premieres can be streamed via Starz.

#8617. Second Air Force National Signing Day Held at U.S. Capitol

When an American joins any branch of the United States military, they repeat an Oath of Enlistment to make the commitment official.

I do solemnly swear that I will support and defend the Constitution of the United States against all enemies, foreign and domestic; that I will bear true faith and allegiance to the same; and that I will obey the orders of the President of the United States and the orders of the officers appointed over me, according to regulations and the Uniform Code of Military Justice. So help me God.

On November 12, 2026, 64 men and women ventured to the Rayburn Office Building of the U.S. Capitol to take that oath and enter the Air Force and Space Force Delayed Entry Program. This swearing-in was the climactic moment of the second annual National Signing Day, an event hosted by the Air Force’s 317th Recruiting Squadron.

The concept of this event came from retired Air Force Master Sergeant and M&F Senior Military Editor Rob Wilkins, who said the idea was inspired by watching his son’s announcement for where he was going to play college football.

Wilkins explained, “I was watching this take place and thought to myself, ‘We should be doing something like this for the military.’”

Wilkins’ idea became a reality thanks to several people he worked with, including Congressman Don Bacon of Nebraska, Air Force Senior Master Sergeant Matt London, and others within the 317th. It made what was already a significant moment in the lives of these future service members even more memorable for them and their families who accompanied them.

Staff Sergeant Maddalyn Secrist was one of the recruiters on-hand for the event and was very involved with making the 2026 event a success. Secrist shared that having this on Capitol Hill took something local to the DMV area and gave it a sense of national awareness.

“It gives it more of a public view and gives these Airmen and Guardians the recognition that they need.”

Prior to their swearing-in, each person’s name was announced as they went to the table to sign on the dotted line and have their photo taken, reminiscent of the high school athletes who announce where they will play in college. Each new recruit was cheered by family, friends, and fellow American citizens as well as members of the Trump Administration like Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for Military Community and Family Policy Stephen B. Simmons and recently appointed Executive Director of the President’s Council on Sports, Fitness, and Nutrition, Jacob Phillips.

Among those new recruits was Kevin McAllister, who was one of the older members of the group. At 35 years old and with a family tradition of service, McAllister knew that being physically prepared was a must, which is why he committed to longer runs and more intense training in preparation for the day. He also had to mentally dedicate himself to the process and suggests others who may be considering service do the same.

“I had to find the right mindset. There was a lot of running and calisthenics, but it taught me how to use different muscles,” he said. Even though he was fully prepared to take the oath, being in the Capitol definitely added a level of gravitas to the day.

“We are surrounded by the place where laws are made. The history of the United States is here. Just getting to add this to my family legacy makes me look at the flag differently.”

Bacon addressed the group and offered words of gratitude and encouragement that could be traced back to his own 30-year military career before entering the House of Representatives. He also shared wisdom that could be beneficial to people from all walks of life, whether they are in the military or not.

“Be the best at the job you’re going to get,” Bacon advised. “Learn that job inside and out so your boss can go, ‘I can trust that person.’”

There is no official word on future Signing Day events, but Secrist hopes that recruiters can use highlights or social media posts from this day to inspire their own applicants and create a similar experience to showcase why being a part of the Joint Force is so special.

Secrist said, “We think other recruiters can see this event and get inspired to do something like this in their own squadrons.”

To learn more about the Air Force or Space Force, go to airforce.com or spaceforce.mil.

#8615. How To Afford a House These Days

The other day, an MMM reader stopped by and left the following comment on one of my older posts about the principles of FIRE:

“While I still find some of MMM’s advice relevant, it seems like every FI blogger out there worked in tech 20 years ago, pulled down a 6 figure salary and bought a house for a bag of potatoes before 2019.

I wasn’t smart enough to find FI when I was young so I sometimes feel like a lot of their advice is not going to help me or others who don’t already own a home and don’t have six- figure salaries in this post-pandemic world.

A lot of the ideas given to young folks are “house hack” “buy a fixer upper” but that is still out of reach and/or complex to navigate with current prices and interest rates. Most townships around me do not want you to chop a house up into ADU’s or multiple units. My cousin owns 60 acres of land but he is not allowed to live on a trailer on that land.

I don’t know what the next generation of FI bloggers will offer, perhaps they are already out there and I just don’t know who they are, but I’d like to hear from them.”–

As with every critique of our ideas, I thought about this comment for a while. Tried to determine if there were any Principles of Mustachianism that were genuinely going obsolete, versus the more common side effects of Complainypants and/or Excuse-itis, two afflictions which have been weighing down our critics since the beginning.

After all, this isn’t the first time FIRE has gone obsolete. Over my retirement I’ve seen it:

Our commenter focuses on two things: the solid salaries of tech workers, and the major increases in house prices (and interest rates) in the most recent four years.

The first one — high salaries in general – is still a factor and I don’t expect that to change. Some jobs just pay more than others, and there’s a lot you can do to increase your income and switch jobs, and I’m all for it. However, ever-increasing income is not my usual focus here on MMM, because I have seen first hand that most people can waste almost any amount of income and still have very little to show for it.

In fact, the very existence of software engineers and doctors and other high earners who are my age and still feeling financial stress is proof of this: it’s mathematically impossible to earn so much for almost 30 years and not have an absolute shit-ton saved, unless you are also spending an absolute shit-ton of money the whole time.

So instead, we focus on how to streamline your spending and live joyfully and efficiently without compromise. We focus on reducing waste, while maintaining or even increasing all of the other benefits that come from spending money more purposefully. These skills are essential even for the highest earners, but they become even more valuable as you move down the income ladder.

So now for the second issue: housing. Does the state of housing here in 2024 screw up the whole FIRE plan?

As with any question, let’s start by looking at the data: how much have US house prices actually risen – adjusted for inflation – since 2019?

It turns out that our own St. Louis Fed makes this extremely useful  information available here.

So there’s our answer: houses “feel” about 25% more expensive right now than they did at the start of 2019 relative to the average salary and the price of everything else. Although interestingly enough,  they are only up about 10% since the last peak in early 2006, a full eighteen years ago! So housing is a blow, but not a FIRE-extinguishing one.

However, this nationwide data masks some much bigger increases in certain popular cities, including my own: Plain old Longmont Colorado now sports a hilariously high $540,000 median home price. So houses are about triple the price they were when I started writing in 2011, which means they’ve risen much faster than the average salary. Which means houses are much further out of reach for the average person in my area.

The solution to this is the same as most other problems: to stop thinking in the way our culture likes to train us (as a victim of outside forces beyond our control) and go back to thinking like a Mustachian.

Houses are just like any other manufactured product, and as such they come at a wide variety of prices, subject to supply and demand.

And just because you happen to live in a certain place (even if you were born and raised there), doesn’t mean you’ll automatically be able to afford to buy a house there. Just as a baby born upon the Apple campus in Cupertino today doesn’t automatically get a new iPhone Pro Max every year.

With every purchasing decision, you need to go through the same series of choices:

So when it comes to houses, you run the numbers, then decide between renting or buying or house hacking. You might start by doing the analysis right in your own city, but also keep in mind that there are lots of other cities and even countries in the world, and there are happy people living in all of them.

But Wait: I don’t want to move to a whole new place!

At this point, people get defensive. We all have ties to our current location, and the stronger the ties the more difficult it becomes to consider moving.

But there’s a difference between genuine, positive bonds to a place and just plain old fear of change. So it’s my job to at least make you question your assumptions, because not doing so is what got you where you are, and it’s also what got our country where it is.

And on a country-wide basis,  I notice that our general fear of relocating creates a very irrational pattern of house prices. They are ridiculously high in some places and ridiculously cheap in others. There does seem to be a general correlation between niceness and cost, but not a perfect one (especially since everyone has their own definition of “nice”)

I moved to Longmont in 2005 because it met our young family’s needs at the time, at the right price with homes about $200,000. Today, at the $540,000 price level (houses average about $450 per interior square foot) it has to compete with a much broader range of cities which offer nicer amenities at equal or lower prices.

Let’s do a hypothetical search using another amazing tool: FRED’s list of the top 1000 metro areas with price per square foot, and plot some of them based on my own judgment of their desirability:

I’m biased towards Colorado because I have so many ties there, and I also highly prioritize sunny climates. My chart suggests that if I wanted to save money, I might start looking around in Albuquerque, whereas Denver would give me a nicer life in the same price range as my current city of Longmont. And if I were willing to spend even more on housing to live somewhere even nicer, I should suck it up and move to Boulder.

Just for fun, I pulled the data from that same FRED website into a separate google spreadsheet (which I’ll share here) and sorted it by cost per square foot. Then, I highlighted a band of affordable cities with housing centered on the $100 per square foot range, which would mean a 2,000 square foot house is about $200k.

As an added bonus, I added a column to calculate the change in house prices over the past year, just in case it helps us see if a city is on the way up or getting cheaper at the moment.

A chart like this is just a starting point – you’d need to read more about any place and then go visit in person before considering a move. But the idea is to start with data, and then do some fun research based on what you learn.

The Earth Awaits: Casting a Worldwide Net

House prices are a valuable metric, because they influence the cost of living more than almost anything else for the typical Mustachian. After all, biking and nature are always close to free, Costcos are available nationwide, and we probably care less than average about the costs of other services like valets and salons.

But there’s still plenty of value in looking at the bigger picture, considering more data points, and also being open to renting versus buying your housing. For this, I’m a big fan of a FIRE blogger-created site called The Earth Awaits, and we can take it for a test drive right now with the following search criteria:

Apartment type: Two bedroom (outside city center)

Temperature range: January lows not colder than 10F

The exact parameters don’t matter too much, as long as you don’t make them too narrow. The important thing is the resulting list, which is meant to give you ideas to research further. For example, that first simple search gave me this list:

Hey, that’s interesting. I like how the site shows the population right on the main list, because that provides a big clue to the “feel” of a city. I personally like the feel of a 50k-200k person town, so I might look into Fayetteville, Columbia or Athens. I’ve also been to Chattanooga and really like that place – who knew it was only about as expensive as Columbus Ohio?

In the end, your physical environment – the people, access to nature, urban features and the weather patterns – is probably the most important factor to get right in creating a happy life. The cost of living there is only one of the factors, and definitely not the most important one.

But if you choose carefully, you can probably slide yourself in the right direction along that “Nice for the Price” scale in order to get more from your life. Even if it just means making a move within your own city to live along a walking path, a little closer to work or to the people or places you care about most.

The key is just to remember that housing is like almost everything in life: It’s a choice that you get to make, and there are great rewards for putting some solid thought and effort into that choice.

Another Fun Example: Doing the Analysis on Tempe/Phoenix Arizona vs Denver

This is a fun exercise, because I’m currently living in the Phoenix area (more on that here)  that is way different than the Denver metro area where I normally live. We can start with the rough measure of housing cost per square foot across each region:

In other words, pretty close. Denver metro* is about 10% higher on average, but the variations from one neighborhood to another within any major city are much larger than that anyway.

So the other factors are more important. Both are surrounded by beautiful mountain recreation and get lots of sunshine, but the climates are famously quite different. Denver is more compact but Phoenix has nicer towns in the foothills around the outskirts.  In the end it’s just personal preference in weighting these various factors, and right now I kind of like the idea of both (Phoenix in winter but Colorado for the other three seasons)

More Adventurous: Let’s Try This in South America!

Going back to The Earth Awaits, if we repeat our earlier search but in South America, we get results like these:

Many of these spots have nice writeups if you click the “Details” button, and if anything sounds right for you, you can go on to learn much more.

It’s true that moving to a new country comes with all sorts of new learning experiences: citizenship and passports, laws and traditions and driver licenses, and of course having to cross an international border every time you want to return to your home country to visit family.

But guess what? If this stuff sounds daunting to you, it’s probably a sign that you need to do it more.

At its core, moving to a new place – even internationally – is just a series of relatively easy Adulting Puzzles. You type stuff into your computer, read the resulting stuff that pops up on your screen, and make the occasional phone call and visit to an official office. I had to do all the same stuff when moving from Canada to the US, alone and just six years out of high school myself.

Sure, it can feel like a “hassle” if you think of it the wrong way, but you know what’s a way, way bigger hassle? Living in a not-very-good place for life, or working an extra 15 years just to afford the higher cost of living in your current city, because you’re too scared to do a few weeks of work to make a big move to a better place.

If a rules-and-paperwork-hater like me can do it, almost anyone can.

While we covered a few examples of actual places in this article, the real purpose was to explain the thought process behind deciding when and where to move. And there are many of you out there besides me who can do the same thing, but better. And we’d love to hear from you!

If you have some favorite cities and countries for good living, or useful techniques for scoping them out, please share them in the comments. I strongly believe that the more we help each other find the right place and enjoy the planet more thoroughly and more efficiently, the better off we’ll all be. So let’s get moving.

* Denver metro on the Fed site includes all the suburbs rather than just the core city which is much smaller and more expensive, but the same is true for the nicer parts of Phoenix so I figure it’s a fair comparison)

I’ve felt similar to the OP about this for a while and I appreciate MMM’s thoughtful analysis and response.

His acknowledgement of the fact that the overall inflation-adjusted US Home Price index masks much much greater increases in many other parts of the country is salient, but I found his follow-on analysis frustrating.

Yes – absolutely – you are *not* entitled to buy a home in whatever location you want just because you live there and believe that you are is not going to get you to FIRE very quickly if at all. He gives his own experience of geographic arbitrage as a good example of how he was able to move somewhere much less expensive than the big city to achieve his goals faster. Plenty of other FIRE types from the MMM age group did the same thing – they moved to Vermont, Bend, Bozeman etc. because those places were affordable and beautiful. The entire point of FIRE is to have the time to enjoy doing what you love and the most FIRE way to do this is by taking on hobbies in the great outdoors.

But here’s the thing: over the last ten years – and especially the last five – beautiful places with access to great low-cost outdoor recreation activities almost all fall into the data that the “US Home Price” graph hides.

Sure you can purchase a home in a climate-ravaged hell-scape or among the rows and rows of flat corn fields this country has to offer for a very reasonable price. Someplace that will make it extremely difficult to do all the many Mustachian things MMM has lauded through the years (biking, parks, outdoors, car-free life, etc.). Food deserts. Bankrupt suburbs or rural towns etc.

I don’t know that I’ve got better advice for these trying times however. I think if it were me, I would probably find a high-paying job in a city with reasonable rents and ease of a non-car lifestyle (funnily enough, in many cities, rents have actually grown at a fraction the rate of real estate). Seattle, Denver, Chicago, Portland, Philadelphia, DC are decent examples of this. NY, Boston, SF, LA, are not. Spend a decade or so (or however long it’ll take you) putting away as much money as you can and then reassess.

Maybe home prices will adjust way down everywhere? Maybe rent forever? Americans hate this idea, but the math makes more and more sense IMO in many parts of the country. Or maybe see if you can find a part of the country that will enable you to live a somewhat Mustachian life with low real estate costs. If it were me, I would be looking at the good parts of the Midwest – Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota. Places resilient to climate change with low housing costs and ample outdoor activities that maybe aren’t as high-brow as those of the wealthy class but still plenty enjoyable.

Sorry this was a bit of a rant, but while I think MMM is doing a lot to brush off the vast difference between the geographic arbitrage available to him and that available today, but I do still thing FIRE is possible for those of us in our 20s!

It’s scary how aggressive some places are getting about denying people’s access to health care and taking away their rights, even the right to travel somewhere else. As Mustachians, we have extra power to vote with our dollars, so we should choose places that care about making people’s lives better.

Agree that geographic arbitrage is the answer, but I do think that the objective quality of the places available for geographic arbitrage 20 years ago is vastly different than today.

One of the big consequences of the internet has been that all the beautiful places of the world (and this country) are simply far better known to everybody. In the 1990s it would have been seen as a very strange decision for somebody from San Francisco to move to (or to even have heard of) Bend Oregon. But now, you wouldn’t blink twice and the real estate market and prices has reflected this “globalization” of local real estate markets.

Still plenty of great places out there though!

I would also propose that folks consider renting indefinitely more seriously. While the cost of purchasing a home has risen quickly in the last decade, rent has (generally) not risen nearly as quickly and renting will give you a lot more flexibility if you decide you don’t love where you’re living! It’s also a nice fixed cost relatively to the risks inherent in home ownership. I’ll caveat that this works a lot better in cities than it does in smaller towns (like Bend) where bad zoning / housing policy has led to restrictions on rental housing propping up prices quite a bit.
