Good point about the bad policy – this seems to be the root cause of almost all the expensive housing in US cities. Whenever you have NIMBYs being allowed to complain to their city councils and get them to block the rezoning and building of new housing on land that THEY DO NOT OWN THEMSELVES, you end up with less new housing and potentially higher housing and rent prices due to the artificially restricted supply.

It is just him and his cat when he is home. The house could easily fit 2 full families with the proper setup. However, getting the approval from the city would likely be impossible.

The larger issue with a redistribution of square footage or other zoning issues would be most people don’t want to buy a multi-family unit. The “American Dream” is not to own a rental unit (for the majority of people), and especially not to rent. Society looks down upon people who don’t own their own homes as failures. It takes a strong independent thinker to not cave to the group think.

The point about internet-generated movement is spot on and really significant. I’ve seen this firsthand in my hometown, which has changed dramatically in the past ten or fifteen years.

As recently as the early 2000s, my hometown was a sleepy seaside town off the beaten path, beautiful but known only by locals and a few others. This was before MapQuest, Google Maps, Zillow, online news, satellite car navigation, etc. If you didn’t already know what it was like there or have a personal connection to tell you, you’d never think to visit or buy property there.

There had always been a community of wealthy seasonal residents with vacation houses on the water, but the rest of the town was solidly middle class or even high blue collar. The local auto mechanics and construction workers lived in town and socialized with the white-collar locals.

But that all changed when the town was “discovered” and people from out of town began outbidding everyone else for the houses. The multigenerational continuity that made the community so strong has been broken by my millennial generation, since most of us couldn’t afford to buy the houses in town that our parents bought. It’s gotten so bad that the school is now at risk of closing for lack of kids, since no young families can afford to live there anymore.

I think that a similar phenomenon is happening at the global level. Housing costs are affected by the (lack of) supply, i.e. NIMBYism, but they’re also affected by demand generated by large-scale immigration. Other things being equal, an influx of new people makes housing more expensive. We see this in some parts of the US, but the effect is stronger in other places like Canada and Australia, where recent unprecedented amounts of immigration have coincided with huge increases in the cost of housing. The internet facilitates immigration by making it much easier for prospective immigrants to see what other places are like and what opportunities are available.

I often say that Philly is an aggressively underrated city if the northeast Megalopolis appeals to you. High speed rail gets you to DC, NY, and Boston. Very reasonable housing prices, and the city is building a ton of new housing stock (but still not enough, rental vacancy rates are too low). You can live in a giant skyscraper condo directly downtown or in a single-family rowhome on the outskirts. You can get a 1200 square foot house for $300-400k in a great neighborhood. Buses and bike lanes abound. Everything is flat and walkable. Good jobs in meds and eds.

I was shocked to learn you can really buy dirt cheap housing in nice, warm areas of this country. His double wide is way bigger than my 900 sq foot bungalow in SF. He bought a nice home for what people pay for annual property taxes here. This isn’t a one-off deal. There are a lot of places in his community like this. No, it’s not a beautiful Victorian, but for someone with limited income, he lives a good life. Now he works part time for the local golf course and get to play golf for free.

Another thing to watch out for is something we might call Irrational Local Driverphobia Syndrome (ILDS):

– it has always worked out just fine. I got where I needed to go. – the residents of EVERY. SINGLE. CITY. have said the same thing: “Oh, it’s not safe to ride bikes HERE.. the drivers here are all crazy, and drinking and driving, and texting on their phone, and they hate cyclists.”

Yes, human-driven cars generally pretty dangerous. But you can mitigate most of that danger by choosing your route carefully, learning bicycle safety and getting lots of practice with bike control through trail and off-road-riding, and very importantly adding super bright flashing lights, front and rear, which you use at all times, sun, rain or shine.

In other words, although cars are the problem, most (although not all) bike crashes could have been avoided if the cyclist were skilled and vigilant enough to provide double the safety and caution – enough to cover both vehicles.

I think anecdotes are best discarded in favor of data. And I tried to do this once a while ago, although this article could use an updating with more recent statistics: https://www.mrmoneymustache.com/2012/06/07/safety-is-an-expensive-illusion/

The summary is that biking is SO GOOD for you, and not really all that dangerous in the big picture, that it has an effectively negative level of danger. i.e. your lifespan and healthspan increase when you do it.

But, if you’re in a rough urban area you gotta treat it like a hockey game where YOU are the puck and every moving thing is trying to hit you. So have the literal flashing lights installed on your bike in all directions, and have your figurative radar running on high as well, especially at every curb cut and intersection.

With proper awareness, you should be able to make it almost impossible for a car to hit you even if they are trying to do so (which of course they aren’t), because you’re riding so defensively.

It sounds harsh, but this is also the same thing it takes to be a good CAR driver and avoid accidents over a lifetime of driving.

I’ve been in IT for close to 40 years, and like a lot of my coworkers majored in something other than Computer Science. I also grew up in the Bay Area, which wasn’t too affordable even then. After a few years of working in Silicon Valley, we moved to Southern California, which at the time was much more affordable and allowed us to purchase our first house. Once the kids were out of the house, we started looking at places to retire, with California being the first choice. I soon realized that you could buy a really nice house in Arizona for about a quarter of the price of something similar in California.

We moved to AZ from CA and now that we’ve been here a while we realize CA is much much nicer. We even live in an area that doesn’t get hellishly hot in the summer (like Phoenix – really hellish)). I wish we had stayed in CA and maybe gone to Sacramento area or further north like Red Bluff. We miss the ocean. Furthermore all the people moving here from CA are driving the prices up so if ya’ll want to move here ya better get going because it isn’t going to last.

Echo your sentiments about Arizona – you pay for what you get. I grew up in CA and have spent a lot of time in AZ. The desert has its own beauty but I don’t like looking at rocks and sand year round. Living in AZ part time during the winter (for North America) is really the way to go, but then you’d need to own two homes and almost double your yearly expenses.

My wife and I happen to live in a paid off house in Wisconsin worth about $450K that we built for $326K 11 years ago.

But this house was built BEFORE I found MMM – had I been a reader of this blog, we would have kept the older new $192K one and been just fine.

I just tallied up our non-house net worth yesterday and we’re at $1.1M. Hopefully I can early retire very soon (age 48 with a rather high paying job, but one that varies throughout any particular day from “great” to “rage quit”).

I’m pleased with our more recent progress, but as we try to clear years of clutter, we’re also finding evidence of silly spending in years past in the form of overstuffed closets, bookshelves, model trains, you name it. Many of which are never used, have never been used, and sort of weigh on you. Facepunch!

And going back further to the start of our marriage, we can both recall our cheap one bedroom apartment, no cable, like 10 audio CDs between us, and our leisure activities being free library books, walking in the adjoining park, and swimming and walking at the YMCA. No restaurant meals, no travel, lots of pasta- and it was great! After getting denied home loans with extreme prejudice (22 years old and 1997 before lending rules became too loose), I tracked every single cent we made or spent on a spreadsheet and within months (6?) we had over $10K saved and bought our first $90K house. I had read “Your Money or Your Life” in college and remembered enough to do that step, though I fell off the wagon later.

If I could somehow send the 22 year old version of me all of the Mr. Money Mustache Classics articles I would, and I still re-read them on a regular basis to help build my “frugality muscle”. No, I don’t need that silly trinket, just like MMM skipped buying the drinking flask. Yes, there is great joy to be had by giving yourself a haircut or making a low cost homemade pizza or taking a brisk walk outside on a very cold, dark night and marveling at stars and planets (all referenced in various MMM articles).

Regardless of how high house prices are, or how much money you make, I believe there is great value in practicing Mustachianism. Striving to save as much money as possible by implementing MMM’s advice in these articles will ALWAYS put you in a better place financially and physical fitness-wise than the opposite.

Thank you, MMM, for writing them – keep ’em’ coming!

My partner and I just moved from Austin, TX to Spartanburg, South Carolina this January. We were both laid off from our jobs last year, but were fortunate to find job opportunities. It seemed like a win-win with higher earning and lower cost of living combo.

There’s not as many highways and it’s’ definitely quieter and calmer here. I’m looking forward to exploring more of the parks around the state as there are many beautiful lakes with hiking trails within a 2-hour drive.

The move was definitely a bit daunting as we didn’t know anyone in the area, and a lot of our friends from school have mostly moved to large cities. I agree I’ve always been surprised how move averse people are. I thought remote work would change that much more than it has.

But, it *is* difficult for people to move if they have a job that requires a particular physical location. And the cost of leaving friends behind shouldn’t be dismissed too lightly. It’s *not* easy at all to make new friends as an adult. We moved after FI’ing in our 30s and still don’t have a friend group as strong as the one we left behind a few years ago.

But also what strikes me is the persistent assumption that everyone needs to own a house. I’ve never owned a house and never even lived in one as an adult. I do own a boat however, which is like a tiny house, that we’ve lived on for 7 years. Renting a small apartment is perfectly valid.

I would suggest to your commenter that he explore the “tiny house/dwelling” movement. Changing the size of your home is often an even easier way to save than location arbitrage. Humans don’t need really need as much space as they think (many average suburban homes feel “mansion-sized” to me).

For example, in my 20s I lived in an 800 sq ft nice apartment and then switched to a 350 sq ft (!!!) studio in a less nice building for a few years, and saved a ton that way.

Totally agree on the not needing as much space as you think. Five years ago I got rid of the last of my things and moved into my (very) minimalist campervan. Five years ago! Not only did I save a ton of money not paying rent, but I got out and saw some of the country while working. On occasion I watch people’s houses while they are away. I must say, houses are so inefficient with their layout, their size, and the way cities are designed around them (almost necessitating cars) that I don’t think I’ll ever own one. I simply can not endorse a design that isolates people from each other making everyone miserable, while at the same time dramatically increasing the cost of living and pollution. To each their own, I guess.

I guess I’m weird but I have never cared much about having friends. Between family, work, and hobbies, I’m covered. Now if a hobby or interest introduces me to someone interesting I’m open to it but otherwise I’m too busy to just “hang out” with people anymore.

I recently bought my first home using the little known hack called “marry an electrician and then get a house with all knob and tube wiring, because no one else will want it due to the wires being old, even though if they were going to burn the house down they likely would have by now.”

Seems to be going very well thus far, and there is a bus at the end of my street which I can take to the city center in 15 minutes for $2.

(I will specify that I did not marry the electrician solely because of their career. They have other qualities.)

Yup. Homes that need remodeling and new plumbing or electrical can be had for hundreds of thousands less in hotter markets. Having the trade or skills to do the work will save so much money.

I’ve added probably between $20k and $75k in value to each of my homes in these ways–always spending way less than the value returned by either doing most of the work myself or contracting out after many bids and significant time considering the design. I’ve never had a house sit on the market. All have gone under contract at about ask or over in a few days or less.

What I’ve appreciated about the Moustachian philosophy (at least from what I can tell) is that it doesn’t assume that we humans deserve to get everything we want and right now!

I’m actually a compulsive debtor in recovery, and reading blogs like this one and books like “Your Money or Your Life,” are very helpful tools for me. My past ridiculous and childish thoughts about money included:

~I deserve this ~Everyone else is doing it, I should be able to as well ~It’s my right ~I shouldn’t have to work and save. I shouldn’t have to sacrifice or make difficult choices.

These thoughts and the silly and financially damaging actions they lead to are not just the affliction of those who are compulsive, but are the foundational philosophy for our consumerist culture.

Just because I live in the U.S., doesn’t mean I deserve to be able to buy a house; especially when I did NOTHING during my pre-recovery days to save for one.

The amazing news is, however, that even though I got into recovery and began to practice sound financial principles only 10 years ago, my hubs and I own a great home in a dream location. We went from overspending each month by about $1,500 (today we’d be almost $250,000 in debt – and that doesn’t include interest payments!) to being worth over $1.5 million (this does include the estimated value of our home).

I work in my dream career and make 2/3 as much money as my hubby, but work 1/4 the time he does (this is the way we both like it).

All this to say that once you turn the ship around, once you begin to change even the smallest behaviors with money to align with Moustachian ideas, it doesn’t take long at all to see HUGE results.

Thanks, Mr. Moustache and all who embrace FIRE and principles of financial sanity! Natalie :^)

I did end up moving and found a whole new and better life!

I had been ‘living’ in San Francisco as a flight attendant in a 3 bedroom with 18 roommates for $375/mo. Since the crew is never there, it wasn’t as uncomfortable but it is the only way that situation worked for the 3 years I did it. I saved a bunch of money and paid off my debts. It also helped socially because our schedules were so wild it was the best way to spend time with people. If I had a bunch of days home I would visit family or friends. My parents were kind enough to store my few items in a spare closet of their house.

I had begun making an excel of places I thought I would like to live and move to then the pandemic hit and it forced me to move as I was laid off. I made a list of requirements including drivable in 2 hours to a major airport/hub or closer if I commuted (I don’t have to go to work every day). It needed to be affordable housing, community-based, good internet (my parents live in Alabama and it’s not available where they live), things for me to do (entertainment), and in a climate with 4 seasons (Alabama has hot or wet, SFO has damp and less damp). I used best places which has a quiz that also asked some other good questions and I decided I probably wanted some kind of university town so there was 24 hour services (because sometimes I work nights) as that would be good for me. I then converted my Honda crv to a van and road tripped and stayed a few days to a week in each area I was considering. When I got to my current town of Harrisonburg Va I fell in love with it. I moved there and bought a house within a few months for $1,100 a month. It needs work since it was built in 1918 but I enjoy that and it has great bones. I put in my transfer to IAD and love it. I later was able to go to a meet up for board gamers which is one of my favorite hobbies. I made a lot of friends and met my husband. Now that I’m back to flying I find I enjoy being home more because I’m not stressed about money since I moved someplace more reasonable and built myself a whole new community for support.

Nice read. I myself have done pretty well with a couple of those strategies: first geoarbitrage in Japan (although I speak the language), then house hacking. On house hacking, I studied up for years on real estate so I get how that may be daunting to some, but for us it’s turned into living for free for 2 years, then more recently choosing to pay half the mortgage to help out family. It takes work, but it will pay off if you put in the effort.

To those who still think house hacking is too hard, there’s a simple solution that’s old as dirt: Get a roommate. Get two even. If owning eventually is part of your dream, put whatever you save in housing expenses into a down payment savings account and pull the trigger once ready. As others have said, the first half of this article (the FRED graph of average sales prices across the US) is statistically questionable and has the feel of “see? housing is actually affordable, you’re just wrong to be looking at actual sales prices in your area”. As you mention, it’s a national average, when all RE markets are local, so it’s unclear what it means at all. Another distortion is that the FRED data comes from FHA, which means that it excludes cash sales and sales with jumbo loans. This distortion tends to result in lower home prices than you see when looking at, say, the Case-Schiller data. Even if you average over the whole country.

But I’m glad I ground through that part because the rest of this has some really practical advice for how to find somewhere to live. There is a classic old Raptitude post “Most Lives are Lived by Default” which suggests that probably your current location is a side-effect of your job, or school, or relationship, and that you could do better if you actively tried to find the “right” location for you. Unfortunately the article provides no advice for _how_ to do this; it mostly suggests moving to a different neighborhood in your current town, with the assumption that you have a good idea of whether you want to be closer/further to nightlife or grocery stores or bike paths or whatever, and you just need to pull the trigger.

But for somebody who is near-FIRE, or “FIRE except for housing”, it’s hard to figure out where to even start. These resources are a great way to filter for locations that are financially reasonable and also in the right part of the country. Another thing I did was keep an eye on r/financialindependence and r/fatfire to see if anybody posted cool understated places to live. Chattanouga popped up, as did Kansas City MO, and Asheville NC.

In 2020 I visited a pile of such cities, as well as big ones like Philly and Portland and NYC, by going on AirBNB and finding a spare room that I could rent for a month or more. In the Portland area I wound up doing this for several months in a row, since it’s a huge place and you can change locations dramatically without leaving the metro area.

When I first started doing this I would always look to stay in whole houses, but this is the wrong approach! Aside from not distorting housing markets by using SFHs as hotels, you actually want to find a place with a host who you can talk to about the city and who can tell you about different neighborhoods. And if you rent spare rooms for long periods, it’s a surprisingly affordable thing to do. Especially as you can often meet people who are willing to let you stay with them without going through a fee-skimming platform like AirBNB.

This strategy might only be practical for single light-travelling digital nomad types but I encourage anybody to seriously consider it.

Thanks for the Albuquerque shoutout! It’s not a perfect place to live, but if you like being outside, it’s hard to do better for what it costs to live here.

FIRE is often about making different choices than everyone else to emphasize the things that really matter to you. You rent a small apartment close to work instead of buying a McMansion in the exurbs. You bike or walk instead of driving a 3-row SUV. You cook at home instead of eating out. You go to the library instead of the movie theater…

…and you move to New Mexico instead of Colorado.

If you’re still working, the national labs are solidly above-average employers that emphasize work-life balance. The outdoor recreation is almost as good as Colorado, and Durango is only a few hours away if you want bigger mountains. There’s a nice airport, a zoo, great museums, and 3 Costcos. The weather is great: cooler than Phoenix in the summer, warmer than Denver in the winter, and sunny almost all the time. Plus, the state is doing lots to support working families, with subsidized daycare and free college tuition.

So if you’re discouraged about how much it costs to live in Bend or Boulder, make less popular choice and check out New Mexico.

As a former Coloradoan, newly adopted New Mexican I can reiterate Joel’s statements. NM isn’t perfect but I feel like I have greater access to outdoor recreation here in NM than I did in the Front Range of Colorado, plus much less people to compete with. There are slightly more sunny days, so I can’t complain about that either.

I’m in Santa Fe, which is pretty comparable to many parts of Colorado regarding cost of living and the weather feels nearly identical to Colorado with our almost 7000′ elevation. Santa Fe punches above it’s weight as a city in regards to culture, restaurants, and museums. There is a good bit of tourism that feeds into that, but the restaurant scene is pretty great. The history of the region keeps me engaged as I continue to learn more about the area.

I keep eyeballing the affordability of Albuquerque and the offerings of a city that is 5x the size of Santa Fe, but Santa Fe fits the bill for now

The key thing, as this article exemplifies, is to EXAMINE both reality, and your own assumptions. So much “can’t afford a house” mania is based on vague unexamined feelings, and vague media-based proclamations. When you cut through that with a bunch of facts and self-examination . . . the world opens up. As this piece shows. In our case, a limiting factor (we thought) was the “must be close to family” idea. Then we realized that 1. family members keep making plans and moving without consulting us, so why base our whole lives on their (temporary) locations? 2. once we did the math and realized how often we “see family” it became clear that 3 visits a year with a couple of family events each time would cover all the hanging-out time we do, anyway. YMMV.

We love to see these people! But in reality, they’re all busy, they move around, and there’s a limit to everyone’s time. So now we are free to live mostly in Europe, where we prefer to be (and where it’s cheap to live a great, low-footprint life), and not feel disloyal because of some presumed idea of “being too far away from family.” We see them as much as ever did! Now it’s just during our annual out-and-back migration. So yeah: really, truly examine everything that seems to be liming your choices.

I think the one thing you missed calling out is how this is especially relevant to FIRE folks who are no longer working. Many of these lower cost cities don’t have the high paying jobs that really helps us along the way.

Personally I went the route of moving to a small apartment and renting in a HCOL city to maximize my income in my younger years. Now that I’m coming up on 40, I’ve moved to a small town in MN and enjoying the much lower cost of living.

The other cool aspect of this idea is that you can live in a very neat neighborhood within these type of towns. For example, I’m living in the heart of the historic neighborhood within walking distance of two lakes and downtown for super cheap. If I had done that in any moderate cost of living city, I’d pay 5-10x as much for housing. So while it’s a small town, it’s still very walkable & bikeable because I’m not stuck out in some suburban wasteland.

#8613. JJ Spaun Got His Swing Back After a Misdiagnosis Nearly Wrecked His PGA Career

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

PGA star John Michael “JJ” Spaun has been at home with the golf clubs since he was gifted that first plastic toy set at age 3. But while the young protégé followed in his mother’s golf-playing footsteps, and furthered them by making progress in the PGA, a mysterious health issue would begin to derail his game.

Spaun sat down with M&F to discuss his initial Type 2 diabetes diagnosis, and how finally being discovered as Type 1 brought him back to greener pastures.

“I would say, in the majority, golf was a pretty easy sport for me to pick up,” says Spaun. “But I think I battled with what time and effort I wanted to put into it as a kid. Growing up in Southern California, other sports were pulling me in. Skateboarding was a huge presence at the time. I wanted to do what the other kids were doing culturally, which was skateboarding and extreme sports.”

In his youth, Spaun played a variety of sports aside from golf, including skateboarding, bicycling, baseball, basketball, and hockey. But while he did eventually fully embrace golf, his other experiences began to pay off. “I think those sports all played a role in my development, in my mechanics,” says Spaun. “Like hand-eye coordination, footwork. My swing coach, who I have been with for around six years, is a firm believer that skateboarding really developed my footwork for my golf swing even as a child. He considers my feet to be my superpower.”

JJ Spaun has just completed his 10th season with the PGA. He turned professional in 2012 and earned his first PGA Tour Card in 2016, but the players’ game began to take a downturn in 2018. He struggled with consistency and even lost his tour card during the 2020-21 season, where he placed 174th in the FedEx Cup rankings. Since the summer of 2018, Spaun found himself almost unable to complete a round of golf.

“I was 28 at the time,” he recalls. “I remember putting on my belt and running out of holes to put the notch in, so my belt was now too big for me. I suffered with severe thirst at night, and then frequently urinating, like, three or four times every night. I started losing weight very rapidly.”

Initially chalking all this up to a demanding golf season, Spaun decided to see a doctor after weighing himself and realizing that he’d inexplicably lost another 20 pounds in just a couple of months. The athlete was diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes and hoped that the treatment would help him return to his prior form on the golf course. But that wasn’t to be.

“After three years, losing 50 pounds, going down to 155 pounds, I hadn’t weighed that since high school, so I finally got advice from an endocrinologist,” shares Spaun, who was then diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes, rather than Type 2.

Sadly, with 90% of diabetes sufferers having Type 2, medical advances for detecting Type 1 have been slower to emerge. Type 2 is often triggered by obesity, whereas Type 1 is thought to be more of a genetic issue causing the immune system to attack insulin producing cells in the pancreas. “They felt sorry for me, telling me that I was Type 1, but I said this is great, because I’ve been living miserably,” says Spaun. “My energy was at an all-time low. My golf was going down the drain. And now I had a real solution.”

Finally gaining the correct diagnosis in 2021, Spaun started insulin therapy. “In a matter of weeks, I could feel the strength coming back,” says the top golfer. “I was able to eat things without restricting my glucose range, as you do with Type 2. I started to feel better and things started coming together.”

Losing so much weight took time to overcome, however. “Your mechanics and your movements are off,” explains Spaun. “I’m glad to be handling things well. It’s definitely a challenge, but I’ve got all the support in the world to really make it as easy for me as possible.”

Incredibly, with the weight coming back and his treatment working well, Spaun had his breakthrough season in 2025, including a major victory at the 125th US Open. Spaun tells M&F that he uses a Dexcom G7 continuous glucose monitor to keep his levels in check and has recently switched from insulin injections to a pump system known as the Omnipod 5. “It’s been a game changer for me,” he shares.

In September 2026, Spaun was also able combine his love of traveling to England with his passion for golf, winning the BMW PGA Championship at Wentworth, and even donating a portion of his winnings to the Addington Fund, a British Charity that supports farming families. The golfer tells M&F that he discovered the financial hardships that many UK farms face during his holidays in the Cotswolds, where discovered the popular Prime series, Clarkson’s Farm.

“I’m the type of guy that likes to put in the work, because I’m a strong believer that you get out of this game what you put in,” says Spaun. But with the official season now over, the able athlete can look ahead to more family time, and another trip back to England.

No doubt, JJ Spaun is a highly decorated athlete with an even promising future, but living with diabetes has taught him that being present in the moment is more important than any trophy, so we conclude our interview and Spaun heads out on the school run.

Mass monster Jay Cutler, who claimed the title of Mr. Olympia on four occasions between 2006 and 2010, was never afraid to step away from the barbell if there was an efficient way to sculpt his back. Recently, the bodybuilder revealed that he liked to begin each back session with cable reverse-grip pulldowns. Here’s why.

“This was always the first exercise I started my back routine with,” confirmed Cutler in a recent video for his 5.7 million IG followers.

Techniques used by Jay Cutler to string together 25 consecutive top 2 finishes.

Utilizing a supinated (underhand) grip, you’ll primarily tax the lats while also recruiting the biceps and mid back. For many, the supinated grip is more comfortable on the shoulders than the pronated (overhand) grip. So, seated at the cable station, you’ll replicate a similar movement with the upper body to a chin up as you lower the bar. This grip also allows for heavier loads, making it perfect for adding upper body mass.

Tip: Keep your torso still and pull with the elbows until the bar is lowered just under your chin. Don’t pull any further down, or the load will shift to your forearms and shoulders.

“When you do something, reverse grip, it’s going to give you more flexion in those lats. It’s going to allow you to pull a little deeper and engage certain fibers,” explained Cutler who, as a competitive bodybuilder, was all about lifting heavy weights to create a winning physique.

In his video, Cutler kept the distance between his hands a little over shoulder width. “Pull down, focus on 12 repetitions,” he added. The Olympia icon also explained that the reverse grip lat pulldown was essential to building the winged appearance of his lats. “So, when I was doing that front double bicep (pose), it really yanked those lats out,” shared the legend. “And created that great V-taper.”

For Jay Cutler, the reverse grip lat pulldown was key to building muscle thickness. To try it for yourself, avoid using momentum and concentrate on the muscle contraction instead, as you lower the bar. Then slowly allow the bar to return skywards for additional time under tension.

With Olympia runner-up Samson Dauda speculated to enter, and Andrew Jacked confirming that he will try to defend his 2026 Arnold Classic trophy, Walker understands that each and every rep counts.

To replicate these reps for yourself, aim for 3 sets of 8 to 12 reps on each exercise. The added weight on the chest dips is optional, but be sure to go heavy, taking in at least one feeler set to avoid injury. This may be a brutal workout, but the muscle building benefits could be brilliant.

#8601. 5 Pain-Free Arm-Building Alternatives to Barbell Curls

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

The barbell biceps curl is arguably a cornerstone of arm day as well as a favorite among gymgoers.

But even with its popularity in the weightroom, there are subtle issues that could come from barbell curl, the main one being a straight bar could be uncomfortable for your wrists.

Unlike dumbbells, which offer more freedom of movement, the barbell doesn’t. That fixed grip might not vibe with your wrists and forearms as the weight gets heavier. With form issues like wrist hyperextension, questionable grip width, and a little too much body English, your wrists may rebel.

This doesn’t mean you should ditch it at the first sign of wrist discomfort. Sometimes, adjusting your grip, cleaning up your form, or checking your ego at the gym door is all that’s needed to start curling without wrist pain.

But sometimes, the barbell and your wrists will not get along.

Next, I’ll break down four common reasons barbell curls strain your wrists and what you can do about it. Then I’ll cover five biceps-building alternatives that let you pump up without the pain.

Here are four common reasons barbell curls bother your wrists and how to fix them.

Unlike dumbbells, a barbell locks both hands in a fixed position. Depending on your forearm anatomy, mobility, and grip width, this position may cause wrist discomfort. A barbell leaves little wiggle room, and your wrists may tell you all about it.

Quick Fix: Adjust your grip width for more comfort, or switch to a reverse grip.

As the load gets heavier or you become more fatigued, wrist hyperextension may happen. Instead of maintaining a wrist and forearm alignment, the bar pulls the hands backward. That adds extra demands on a body part that’s already working hard.

Quick Fix: Think knuckles in line with your forearms, and do a partial wrist curl to get your hands in that position.

There’s a time and place for body English, but if it causes unnecessary discomfort by pulling your wrist out of neutral during the curl, reconsider your strategy.

Quick Fix: Lighten the load, cut the set short when excessive momentum takes over, or use a three-second eccentric to slow things down.

Your forearms stabilize your wrists, and if you’ve already done a lot of grip work, your wrists may be tired before you begin. When your forearms and wrists fatigue, your grip may weaken, your wrist position may change, and your biceps will be left unsatisfied.

Quick Fix: If your grip gives out, do direct biceps work earlier in your workout with lighter loads, different grip positions, or the alternative exercises below.

If the form fixes didn’t work, it’s time for the alternative. A good alternative trains the biceps hard while addressing what made barbell curls uncomfortable in the first place.

Angled grips, neutral grips, and even overhand grips may feel better depending on your wrist and forearm anatomy. For example, an EZ bar reduces the amount of supination required, while hammer curls keep your palms facing each other.

Dumbbells, ropes, and resistance bands give your hands and wrists more freedom of movement than a barbell.

Look for exercises that keep your wrists neutral, let you control the lifting and lowering phases, and maintain biceps tension. Dumbbells, cables, and bands each feel different but may let you control the weight better without sacrificing gains.

The bottom line: A good barbell curl alternative should solve your wrist problem without creating a new one.

With that covered, here are five exercises that let you keep building bigger biceps without being married to the barbell.

Each exercise addresses one or more of the problems we discussed earlier, so choose wisely. Also, keep a mirror handy.

Solves: Wrist discomfort from the barbell’s fixed position.

The EZ-bar curl is the closest alternative to the barbell curl without locking the wrist in place. Its angled handles allow your forearms to sit in a slightly more neutral position, which many lifters find more comfortable than the barbell.

Form Tip: Choose a hand position that feels comfortable, and keep your wrists neutral.

Solves: Discomfort from the palms-up grip.

If you’ve been hammering the palms-up position, it’s time to switch. Using a palms-down grip shifts the exercise’s emphasis, placing greater demand on the brachioradialis and brachialis while the biceps still get the attention they deserve. The reverse curl provides a different stimulus and gives you another grip option if wrist pain is an issue.

Form Tip: Keep your elbows close to your sides, curl without body English, and lower with control.

Solves: The difficulty of keeping your wrists aligned during barbell curls.

The rope-cable hammer curl combines the wrist-friendly benefits of the dumbbell hammer curl with a touch of cable magic. This variation gives your wrists and hands more wiggle room, letting you adjust your hand spacing throughout the curl. The cable also provides constant resistance throughout the range of motion, enhancing biceps development.

Form Tip: Attach a rope to a low cable pulley and stand tall with your palms facing each other. Curl the rope toward your shoulders, then let your hands separate at lockout.

Solves: Wrist discomfort from a barbell’s fixed grip.

If barbell curls hurt your wrists, the answer may be to lighten the load and switch resistance types. That’s where the looped resistance band curl earns its place. Unlike a barbell, which provides the same external weight throughout the rep, a resistance band’s resistance increases as it stretches.

And don’t mistake bands for beginner-only equipment. Take a challenging set to near muscular failure with good form, and your biceps will thank you.

Form Tip: Grip the sides with your preferred grip, keep your wrists aligned, and curl toward your shoulders. Lower slowly without letting the band snap your hands back.

Solves: Wrist discomfort from limited freedom of movement.

Unlike a barbell, dumbbells let you rotate your forearms as you curl, moving from a neutral grip at the bottom to a palms-up position near lockout. This rotation is more joint-friendly while still engaging the biceps’ two primary functions: elbow flexion and forearm supination.

Form Tip: Start with dumbbells at your sides, palms facing inward. As you curl one dumbbell toward your shoulder, rotate your palm up. Squeeze your biceps at the top, lower under control, and repeat with the opposite arm.

Sets & Reps: 2–4 sets of 12-15 reps per side

Your biceps cannot tell the difference between a barbell, dumbbell, resistance band, or cable machine. They only care about tension. If that tension comes from a barbell and your wrists are annoyed, why keep hammering it when you have options?

If the form fixes above didn’t work, these five alternatives will help you train for gains without the pain.

#8599. Ryan ‘Koup’ Kuperus Shares How the Reason Outdoors is Saving Lives and Building a Community

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

The mission for The Reason Outdoors is to take veterans, first responders, and their children on outdoor adventures such as hunting or fishing as a positive experience that can help enhance their quality of life.

The organization was founded by three veterans, Ryan Kuperus, Tony Cowden, and Andrew Somplasky. Kuperus is also President of The Reason Outdoors, and he feels that what he does now benefits himself as much as it does the people they take on these adventures.

“I really take pride in seeing veterans and first responders and especially their kids harvest their first animal to see that joy and happiness. It’s just fantastic.”

The connections between the members of The Reason Outdoors team and the over 300 people they work with go beyond the benefits of hunting and fishing. They also understand the pressures that come with service, the search for a purpose when the uniform comes off, and the struggles that go along with them. Kuperus doesn’t need to question whether their efforts make a difference. They get told first-hand about the impact they have had.

“We have had five guys tell us, ‘If it wasn’t for this hunting trip or this fishing trip, I would have put a pistol in my mouth and pulled the trigger.”

Kuperus could have gone into farming like his father before him, but he felt the move for him was to join the military. He joined the Marines in August 2000. By the end of 2001, he was a part of the first deployment following the September 11th terrorist attacks. In 2003, the then 20-year-old was a squad leader during the invasion of Iraq, which he considered a career highlight.

“As a squad leader, that is a very respected position to be able to lead men in combat,” he said. “I had a guy in my squad who was 37 years old. That was pretty big for me.”

Throughout his 17-plus-year career, he would travel to Iraq, Japan, and the Philippines as well as Afghanistan. At one point in his career, he broke his femur and fractured his forehead in a Humvee rollover. Nonetheless, he rehabbed and eventually returned to action, including a return to Afghanistan.

Gunnery Sergeant Kuperus’s career ended via medical retirement in 2017. The Purple Heart and Navy Commendation Medal with Valor recipient was looking for another way to make a difference. While he was recovering from his rollover accident, he took up bow hunting and said he found healing while he was in the woods. He never let go of that connection and leaned into it even more after his career ended by going on organized hunts with other groups.

Kuperus recalled, “I had the opportunity to go on a couple of Wounded Warrior hunts and Purple Heart hunts and stuff and had a great time with some awesome organizations.”

Kuperus went on to start Hunting Carolinas, a part-time guide service. In 2022, Kuperus, Cowden, and Somplasky then started The Reason Outdoors. This wasn’t just another job for “Koup,” it was helping him as much as it was those they took on trips.

“We were off to the races,” he said. “I found healing in the outdoors, in nature, and through hunting.”

Kuperus found personal healing in the woods, but his experience is far from anecdotal. Science increasingly backs what veterans discover around the campfire. A pilot study published in 2013 found that combat veterans suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder experienced noticeable reductions in stress and PTSD symptoms after participating in group-based outdoor recreation programs. There are physical benefits of the outdoors as well. A report in 2018 confirmed that increased exposure to natural outdoor environments was statistically associated with significant reductions in diastolic blood pressure, heart rate, and salivary cortisol levels.

Kuperus and his teammates not only take their clients out on trips. They teach them the skills needed for harvesting so they can apply them later on. Cowden provides workouts on his social media for others to use, and they are actively engaged with their followers. They are looking to provide more than a one-off experience. They have been planting the seeds for a community, and that community is growing. Kuperus sees the results of their efforts for himself every time he looks at a fellow veteran or first responder that they go out with.

Kuperus stated, “Somebody there was feeling down before that hunt. Now they’ve expanded their network. The camaraderie brought the light back to their eyes, so to speak.”

Kuperus and everyone with The Reason Outdoors will continue their mission because they know how important and supportive their work can be. He hopes that other veterans will find their own ways to continue serving or reach out for help if they are in a dark place like he and others he knows have been in. Focusing on mental, physical, and spiritual fitness are key for veterans and their families, and Kuperus advises that if any or all of those aspects are not optimal, addressing it in a positive way is crucial.

“That’s probably the hardest thing for a veteran to do is to admit how dark a path they’re on. So, don’t let yourself get to that point. Start by talking to somebody and get it out. That alone is a start and helps a lot.”

#8590. Hany Rambod Shares His Top Rule For Building Wider Shoulders

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Wide shoulders are a staple for anyone looking for a fit physique, but if you take the wrong approach to training them, you could be growing your trapezius instead of your deltoids. Fortunately, the coach they call “The Pro Creator” has shared one of the secrets that helped him win 25 Olympia’s for his legendary clients, and it’s a lot simpler than you might think.

Whether you are a competitive bodybuilder, or just want to look more “alpha,” then wider shoulders are a much sought after physical attribute. The shoulders contain the deltoid muscle group and often work in combination with the trapezius muscle towards the neck, and the triceps in the arms. To help isolate those gains, shoulder training requires specific exercises such as the overhead press, lateral raises, rear delt flies, and front delt raises, but the way that you execute these movements is paramount to your success.

“The key for shoulders is not to train too heavy,” explained Rambod, who has guided the likes of Phil Heath, Jay Cutler, Hadi Choopan, and Derek Lunsford towards bodybuilding gold. “Because if you go heavy, your traps kick in.” In other words, putting too much strain on your shoulders can lead to the recruitment of the trapezius muscles that are located in the upper back and neck. “If you’re really trying to build your delts, you really want to make sure that you’re not going light, but you’re using medium to heavier weight, without swinging.”

While we are often told that “more is more” as relates to lifting weights for muscle growth, scientific research has shown that significant muscle gains can occur at just 40% of your one rep max, particularly if a higher volume of reps is added. While you may want to go heavier than that, or stick within the 8- to 12-rep range, the truth is that whatever weight you engage, any exercise will be inefficient if proper form is not practiced.

“Once you swing, you engage the traps,” said Rambod, explaining why moving with the momentum could cause you to miss the muscle building potential inside the shoulders. “And, if you’re traps get too big, it actually can make you look more narrow.” Of course, he’s right again. A thick neck can make the shoulders look out of proportion, and appear slimmer, and this is the opposite of the effect you should be aiming for.

For competitive bodybuilders, failing to get the balance correct will result in a lesser score from the judges. “If you’re gonna be bodybuilding and you’re trying to get on stage at some point, you really want to make sure you balance the trap size with the thickness of the delts, so therefore you maximize your width.”

Take home message? “It’s not about how much weight you move, it’s about where you’re putting the tension,” wrote Rambod in his caption. “Keep the traps out of the movement, focus on your delts, and make every rep counts.”

#8589. Hyatt Category 4 Free Night Certificate — Card Perk Sweet Spot

Withdrawal plans, Roth ladders, and early access.

Index funds, asset allocation, and real estate.

Roth conversions, capital gains, and FI tax planning.

Career growth, side hustles, and entrepreneurship.

Beliefs, purpose, and financial psychology.

Exercise, nutrition, and mental wellness.

The simplest high-value card perk in travel rewards — no points math required

Picture this: you walk into a stunning hotel lobby — maybe it's the Hyatt Regency Kyoto, maybe it's the Andaz Maui at Wailea, maybe it's a chic Hyatt Centric in the heart of a city you've always wanted to explore. You hand over your World of Hyatt card at check-in, and the night is on the house. Not because you're a high roller. Not because you spent $50,000 on a credit card. Because you crossed a spending threshold you were hitting anyway, and Hyatt rewarded you with a free night certificate that covers any Category 1–4 property in the entire portfolio. This is what the ChooseFI community means when we talk about travel rewards done right: identifying the moments where a credit card benefit perfectly intersects with your normal life, and extracting maximum value with minimum complexity. ## The Math That Makes This a No-Brainer Here's the value proposition in plain numbers. Category 4 Hyatt properties — places like the Thompson Nashville, the Hyatt Regency Maui, or the Andaz San Diego — regularly command **$200 to $400 per night** in cash. On peak dates, holiday weekends, or in premium markets, that number climbs even higher. Your free night certificate covers any of these properties at no additional points cost. None. Zero. This isn't a discount. It's a full, unrestricted free night at properties that charge real-world luxury rates. Why does this represent a genuine pricing inefficiency? Because Hyatt's Category 1–4 certificates are earned through a flat spending threshold — $15,000 on the World of Hyatt Credit Card in a calendar year — and can be redeemed at properties whose nightly rates vary enormously. A Category 4 certificate costs the same to earn whether you use it at a $150 roadside property or a $400 resort. The system rewards you for targeting the high end of the range every single time. For a household already putting everyday spending on a rewards card, $15,000 across a full calendar year is often an achievable benchmark. Groceries, utilities, insurance premiums, quarterly tax payments — it adds up faster than you think. And when it does, Hyatt drops a certificate in your account that can deliver **$300–$400 in hotel value** without spending a single additional point. In the World of Hyatt program — consistently rated the **best hotel loyalty program for value per point** — this certificate is one of the most quietly powerful perks on any hotel card in the market.

The core mechanism here isn't a transfer partnership exploit or a routing rule loophole. It's simpler and more durable than that: Hyatt's Category system creates a ceiling, not a floor. When you earn a Category 1–4 free night certificate, you're not locked into a $150-a-night budget motel. You're handed a key that opens any door in that range — and some of those doors lead to genuinely spectacular properties.

Hyatt operates on a fixed award chart, ranging from 3,500 points for a Category 1 night all the way up to 45,000 points for a Category 8 night. Unlike programs that use dynamic pricing (where award costs swing with cash demand), Hyatt's chart is static. A Category 4 property costs the same 15,000 points whether it's a Tuesday in February or New Year's Eve.

Your free night certificate functions exactly like those 15,000 points — but you earned it through card spending, not through a points balance. This means the certificate has a defined and predictable value: whatever a Category 4 property charges in cash on the night you use it is exactly what you're getting for free.

The pricing inefficiency exists because Hyatt assigns categories based on average nightly rates across the year — but peak-season rates at desirable Category 4 properties can blow well past that average. A Hyatt Regency in a major city might be Category 4 because its average annual rate qualifies, but on a conference weekend or holiday weekend, that same room might cost $350–$400. Your certificate captures that peak-season value without any upcharge.

While this sweet spot is certificate-based (no points required), World of Hyatt integrates beautifully with two major transferable currency programs:

This matters for your broader strategy. If you want to stack a certificate with a separate points redemption — say, booking multiple nights where the first is covered by the certificate and subsequent nights use transferred points — you have two strong, flexible on-ramps into the Hyatt ecosystem. Chase Ultimate Rewards is the workhorse of the FI community's travel rewards stack, and having Hyatt as an instant 1:1 partner makes it one of the most actionable transfer relationships in the game.

Hyatt charges no fuel surcharges on award redemptions — a meaningful distinction compared to some airline programs where surcharges can swallow most of your savings. Your certificate redemption is clean: one certificate, one free night, no surprise fees at checkout beyond standard resort fees (which, to be fair, do apply at some properties — more on that in Pro Tips).

World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. As a World of Hyatt Credit Card holder, your card activity will naturally keep your account active, so expiry is rarely a concern for cardholders. But if you ever cancel the card, make sure you use your points and certificates before they age out.

Booking a World of Hyatt free night certificate is genuinely one of the easiest processes in all of travel rewards. Here's the complete walkthrough from certificate to check-in.

Log in to your World of Hyatt account at hyatt.com and navigate to your account dashboard. Under the "My Certificates & Awards" section, confirm your Category 1–4 free night certificate is present and note its expiration date. Certificates are typically valid for 12 months from issuance, so don't let it sit unused. If you don't see it and you've crossed the $15,000 annual spend threshold on your World of Hyatt Credit Card, allow a few days for it to post after your statement closes, or call Chase to confirm.

Go to hyatt.com and use the hotel search function. You can filter by World of Hyatt category — specifically, search for Category 4 properties in any destination you're targeting. Don't shortchange yourself by defaulting to a Category 1 or 2 property out of habit. The certificate works at any Category 1–4 property, so always target the top of the range. Look for properties with high nightly cash rates — this is where your certificate delivers the most value.

Once you've identified a target property, search your dates on hyatt.com and switch the search to "Use Points." Category 4 properties will show award availability for 15,000 points per night. If award availability shows for that date, your certificate will cover it. Hyatt's booking window opens 395 days in advance, so for peak travel dates — holidays, major events, popular travel seasons — you can and should book the maximum window out.

Proceed through the booking process. At the payment step, you'll see an option to "Apply Free Night Award" or select your certificate from your account. Select the Category 1–4 certificate. The system will apply it and your total cash charge drops to $0 for the room rate (plus taxes and any applicable resort fees).

Hyatt award availability at popular properties can be limited during peak periods. Your tactical options:

Hyatt operates on a fixed category system where each property is assigned a category from 1 to 8 based on the brand and location, not the current market rate. This creates a structural pricing inefficiency: a Category 4 property in a high-demand market like Maui or Kyoto charges the same certificate cost as a Category 4 in a mid-tier city. Your free night certificate works at all of them equally. Unlike hotel programs with dynamic pricing where the cost of a free night fluctuates with demand, Hyatt's fixed chart means you can target the highest-value Category 4 properties without paying more. The card's $95 annual fee is one of the lowest in the premium hotel card category, yet the certificate alone delivers $250 to $400 or more in value — a return that makes the math trivially easy for any FI-minded household.

Let's make this concrete with a real example that represents exactly how this certificate shines.

The Andaz San Diego is a boutique lifestyle hotel in the Gaslamp Quarter — rooftop pool, stylish rooms, walking distance to everything downtown. It's the kind of hotel that signals a real trip, not just a place to sleep. On a standard weekend night, cash rates run $250–$350 per night. During Comic-Con, a Padres playoff weekend, or a major convention, rates push past $400.

Cash cost: $300 (conservative weekend estimate) Certificate cost: 0 points, 1 Category 1–4 free night certificate Your out-of-pocket: $0 for the room rate

You earned this certificate by crossing $15,000 in annual spending on the World of Hyatt Credit Card — a threshold many households reach through regular everyday spending over 12 months. The certificate posts automatically, you search availability on hyatt.com, and you apply it at checkout in about five minutes.

You're not redeeming into a budget experience. The Andaz brand sits at the upper-upscale tier of the Hyatt portfolio. You check in through a host model (no formal front desk), settle into a room with thoughtful design, and wake up knowing that $300 night cost you nothing extra beyond your normal spending.

If you hold World of Hyatt elite status — Discoverist, Explorist, or Globalist — that status applies to certificate bookings exactly like paid stays. Room upgrade requests, early check-in, late check-out: all the same benefits apply.

In every case, your one certificate delivers more value than most points redemptions in any hotel program. And you earned it without touching your points balance.

Your certificate works identically at a $150/night Category 4 property and a $400/night Category 4 property. Always search for the properties with the highest cash rates in your target destination. Use hyatt.com's rate display to compare award availability against current cash pricing — this directly shows you the value you're capturing.

Hyatt's booking window opens 395 days in advance. For properties in high-demand markets — Maui, New York, Chicago during peak season — award inventory gets claimed fast. Set a calendar alert to search exactly 395 days before your target dates and book the moment the window opens.

Your certificate covers one night. If you're staying multiple nights, stack it strategically: apply the certificate to the highest-cost night (often a Saturday) and book the remaining nights with World of Hyatt points transferred instantly from Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt Rewards at a 1:1 ratio. This hybrid approach maximizes the value of every currency you're using.

World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of inactivity. As a cardholder, your spending activity resets this clock automatically. But if you ever pause card use, make a small Hyatt purchase — even a $1 on-property charge — to reset the timer and protect your balance.

Hyatt does not waive resort fees on award and certificate bookings at all properties. Before booking, check whether your target property charges a daily resort fee — these can run $25–$50/night and will appear on your final bill. Factor this into your value calculation, especially at resort properties in Hawaii or Las Vegas.

The $15,000 spend threshold should come from natural household spending, not manufactured purchases. In the FI community, we optimize around spending you're doing anyway — insurance premiums, tax payments, groceries, utilities. If you're buying things you don't need to hit the threshold, you're eroding the value of the certificate.

Certificates issued by Hyatt are typically valid for 12 months. Mark the expiration date in your calendar the moment the certificate posts. An expired certificate is $300+ in value that simply disappears — one of the most painful mistakes in travel rewards.

This sweet spot is built for the everyday FI household that's already spending $15,000 or more annually on a single credit card and wants to redirect that activity toward a meaningful travel benefit. You don't need a large points balance. You don't need to understand transfer partners or award chart math. You earn the certificate by spending, you apply it at checkout, and you get a free night at a genuinely nice hotel.

You need: the World of Hyatt Credit Card, $15,000 in annual card spending, and a World of Hyatt account. No minimum points balance required — this is a card perk, not a points redemption.

If your annual spending is significantly below $15,000 on a single card, this particular mechanism won't trigger. In that case, the World of Hyatt Credit Card still earns Hyatt points on spending and delivers a Category 1–4 certificate on each card anniversary — so it retains value, just through a different path. Also, if you're deeply committed to a non-Hyatt hotel program, the benefit is obviously less useful without a library of Hyatt properties in your regular rotation.

## Rated: Easy (4/5 Beginner Friendly) This is one of the most accessible sweet spots in the entire travel rewards ecosystem, and that's by design. The certificate mechanism removes the two biggest friction points in traditional points redemptions: **finding the right number of points** and **navigating complex transfer timing**. You earn the certificate passively through spending, it posts to your account automatically, and the booking process on hyatt.com is as intuitive as booking any other hotel stay. ## What Makes It Easy - **No transfer required** — the certificate lives in your World of Hyatt account, ready to apply at checkout - **Fixed pricing** — Category 4 is Category 4 everywhere in the world; no dynamic pricing surprises - **Simple availability search** — hyatt.com's award search is clean and straightforward ## The One Genuine Challenge: Availability at Popular Properties The only real friction point is award inventory at high-demand Category 4 properties on desirable dates. Hyatt limits how many award rooms it releases per night, and popular properties in destinations like Hawaii or New York fill quickly. **Three ways to beat this:** 1. Search 395 days in advance when fresh inventory releases 2. Build a shortlist of 3–5 Category 4 properties in your target region so you have backup options 3. Stay flexible on dates — midweek nights almost always have more award availability than weekends If you can approach this with even modest date flexibility, you will find great options. The Hyatt portfolio at Category 4 is large and geographically diverse, and there is almost always a compelling property available somewhere you'd actually want to go. For anyone new to travel rewards, this certificate is the perfect first redemption — low complexity, high reward, and a genuinely memorable hotel stay to show your household what this strategy can deliver.

Log in to hyatt.com and check My Certificates and Awards after your card anniversary. Note the expiration date — certificates are typically valid for 12 months. If it does not appear within a few weeks of your anniversary, contact Chase.

Search hyatt.com for Category 4 hotels in your target destinations. Compare the cash rate against the free certificate value. Target properties where cash rates exceed $300 per night — these deliver the highest return on your $95 annual fee.

Hyatt opens its booking window 395 days in advance. For popular Category 4 properties in Maui, New York, or Kyoto, set a calendar reminder and book the day the window opens. Apply your certificate during the booking process on hyatt.com.

Use the free night certificate for the most expensive night of your stay (typically weekends or peak dates), then book remaining nights with World of Hyatt points at 15,000 points per Category 4 night. This combination stretches your overall lodging value significantly.

Category 4 includes well-known properties like the Andaz Maui at Wailea, Hyatt Regency Kyoto, Andaz San Diego, Hyatt Centric locations in major cities, and many Thompson hotels. The full list is available on hyatt.com by filtering the award chart. Category 4 is the sweet spot tier where property quality is high but the award cost remains accessible.

The World of Hyatt credit card automatically issues a Category 1-4 free night certificate each year on your card anniversary. A second certificate is earned after you spend $15,000 on the card in a calendar year. No special action is required beyond holding the card and meeting the spending threshold for the bonus certificate.

Yes. The free night certificate is valid for any available standard room at a Category 1-4 property, including weekends and holidays. There are no blackout dates. However, standard room availability may be limited during peak periods, so booking early is recommended.

The certificate expires 12 months after issuance and cannot be extended or refunded. If you know you will not use it, consider booking a refundable reservation at a Category 4 property to hold the value, then cancel and rebook if your plans change. Do not let it expire unused — the value easily exceeds the annual fee.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

The Hyatt Category 4 free night certificate is the most accessible sweet spot in travel rewards. You do not need to understand transfer partners, award charts, or complex booking strategies. You hold the World of Hyatt credit card, the certificate arrives on your anniversary, and you redeem it at a hotel where cash rates run $250 to $400 or more per night. The $95 annual fee pays for itself three to four times over with a single use. For FI-minded households that consolidate $15,000 or more in annual spending on one card, the second certificate doubles the value. This is the card perk that turns skeptics into believers — simple math, real savings, no tricks required.

#8586. Andrew Jacked Shares His Back-Building Training Ahead of the Arnold Classic

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

With fans and competitors now looking to the 2027 Arnold Classic for the next big battle of the bodybuilding titans, last year’s winner could take to the stage with an even more impressive back. Recently, Chinedu Andrew Obiekea, who is better known to flex fans as “Andrew Jacked,” shared his training process—and it was boss level.

Undoubtedly, 2026 was a breakout year for the Nigerian French competitor. First, Jacked won the biggest prize in bodybuilding history, picking up a check for $750,000 for winning the Arnold Classic in Columbus, Ohio. Then days later, the big man won the Arnold UK, and picked up another $250,000 for his efforts. But with current and former Mr. Olympia’s like Nick Walker, Hadi Choopan, and potentially Samson Dauda hot on his heels, AJ is now in the process of jacking up his back to maintain his top position with the judges.

AJ jolts his back to adapt with this simple but seriously heavy workout.

“Yesszziirrr!!!,” came the trademark quote from AJ, as he shared his herculean efforts for more than a million followers on Instagram. Here’s how to try it for yourself:

AJ began with an unorthodox but rewarding version of the bent over row. Rather than use a dumbbell or barbell, the “Mona Lisa of bodybuilding,” stood behind the chest support on a T-bar row machine, gripping the frame for support, while taxing his working arm independently. By following the strict path of the machine, AJ maximized the load and strengthened his middle and lower trapezius (below his neck), while also building thickness in the side of his back working the lats and teres minor and major.

With his back now suitably blasted, Jacked continued the onslaught with the traditional standing barbell bent over row. Using a pronated (overhand) grip, AJ once again targeted the lats while also building his mid and upper back. Next up was the chest supported mid row, zeroing in on the upper back, including the traps and rhomboids (located between the shoulder blades and spine) Notice, in all of Andrew Jacked’s movements, how he likes to extend his arms to the very bottom of each lift, in order to find a maximum stretch before contracting his gigantic muscles. The lats then took another licking with cable lat pulldowns, while seated cable rows hit all the major muscle groups in the back.

To strengthen his posterior chain, Jacked performs back extensions at a 45-degree angle, building the entire back, glutes, and even his hamstrings. This exercise is particularly savvy, because it supports lumbar stability, improves hip mobility, and means that his other lifts may benefit while maintaining longevity to boot. To work his back even harder, the 2026 Arnold Classic champ pics up some weight plates to take with him on each extension.

When you attack the back from all angles, you will also recruit additional muscles, so to round out his session, Jacked focuses on his already stimulated biceps, and reps out some preacher curls to isolate his arms into exhaustion.

To try this workout for yourself, aim for 8 to 12 reps and perform 2 to 3 sets of each exercise. For the back extensions, start out without the extra weight, and bring it on when you feel comfortable. Yesszziirrr!
