In an example from Forbes, we see two 25-year-old savers earning identical salaries. One enrolls immediately at a 10% deferral rate with a 3% match. The other waits five years, then contributes 6% to capture the same 3% match.

The second saver’s fund even outperforms the first, returning roughly 8.9% annually versus 8.4%, partly from a private equity allocation meant to make up lost ground.

By 65, the early starter still ends up with roughly $3 million, compared with $2 million for the saver who waited. That $1 million gap comes from two things: five fewer years of compounding and a lower savings rate (9% of pay versus 13%). The higher return didn’t come close to closing it. If you’re still in training, here’s what to set up now.

As you can see, when it comes to retirement savings, your timing often matters more than any other variable.

A dollar contributed at 25 has decades to compound and no later contribution, however large, can fully make up for a late start. The 401(k) is also one of the few accounts you can start on day one without worrying much about what happens when you change jobs.

That’s because, as opposed to pensions and employer-funded bonus plans, the 401(k) is portable. Your own contributions are yours the moment they hit your account, and they go with you when you leave. Employer matches can be different. Many plans vest the match over time, either all at once after up to three years or gradually over up to six.

Leave before you’re vested and you lose the unvested part, so check your plan’s vesting schedule before you time a job change. You can roll it into a new employer’s plan or an IRA, and it will continue to compound without interruption.

Benna may not be happy with how his invention turned out, but for me, looking at how it has created a new class of millionaires, it is the one non-negotiable account in retirement planning for physicians and beyond.

Also read: One Big Beautiful Bill Act: What It Means for Physician Taxes in 2025 and 2026

The IRS caps employee contributions at $24,500 for 2026. Workers 50 and older can add an $8,000 catch-up, and those between 60 and 63 get a larger $11,250 “super” catch-up instead, bringing their total to $35,750.

No. More than 80% of employers who sponsor a 401(k) offer some form of match, but the formula varies. Some match dollar for dollar up to a set percentage of salary, others match 50 cents on the dollar to a higher threshold.

Yes. A 401(k) invests in the market through mutual funds or target-date funds, so balances can drop during downturns. Over decades, though, contributions and compounding have historically outpaced short-term losses for most savers.

It depends. A 401(k) is portable, so you keep the balance and can roll it into a new employer’s plan or an IRA when you switch jobs. A pension pays guaranteed income for life, but most of the benefit builds in your later years with one employer, so people who change jobs often come out behind.

Yes. Directing more of a couple’s combined savings toward whichever spouse has the richer employer match captures free money that even splits often miss, sometimes adding thousands to household retirement savings with no extra out-of-pocket cost.

Yes, if your 2025 wages from the employer sponsoring your plan topped $150,000. Your catch-up contributions must go in as Roth. Partners paid through K-1 income aren’t affected.

You keep everything you contributed yourself, plus any match that has already vested. The unvested part goes back to the plan.

Nearly. Both have the same $24,500 limit for 2026 and the same catch-up rules. A 403(b) is offered by nonprofits like hospitals and universities, and some have fewer investment options.

Those who make more money can also save more money. Shocker.

Once you retire and accumulate enough to support the life you want, it’s likely your priorities will change. You won’t need to squeeze every last dollar of growth from your portfolio. You might be more focused on making what you’ve built last.

“The only purpose of money is to build the life you want.” What does it say about you if some of your happiest memories are those during which you didn’t have much money?

Happiness starts out higher when you’re young, dips in middle age and then goes back up in your older years. The thing about the happiness curve is you overestimate your future life satisfaction when you’re young and underestimate your future happiness when you’re in middle age. Both feelings are probably wrong but impossible to ignore.

Everybody wants to argue about what AI is going to do tomorrow. Which jobs will disappear? Which companies will lose? What happens to the people who get left behind? Those are fair questions. But what about the jobs that don’t exist yet? What about the industries nobody has invented? What about the opportunities we can’t even imagine today?

Renting comes with uncertainty. You might have to move, you’re subject to someone else’s rules, and you have less autonomy over your living space. Homeownership, meanwhile, is presented as stability, security, and a permanent place for your children to grow up. Sounds perfect. But where are the property taxes, maintenance bills, unexpected repairs, and time spent dealing with contractors? What about the opportunity cost of tying up a substantial portion of your net worth in a single, illiquid asset?

Retirees sometimes tap savings for one-off expenses. Withdrawing money from a traditional 401(k) or individual retirement account is not as simple as taking the amount you need, advisors say. There are tax implications to consider that go beyond owing taxes on the money you withdraw.

Many adult children are ignoring the old adage “don’t count your chickens before they hatch,” and conducting their finances based on an inheritance they may not receive. Baby boomers are sitting on a pile of wealth, and some researchers estimate they’ll have to pass about $124 trillion of that in what’s dubbed the “Great Wealth Transfer” to next generations through 2048. Others, though, warn potential heirs not to get their hopes up.

Financial silence creates immense, unnecessary suffering. The administrative scramble piled on top of deep grief is enough to break a family apart. So why do we wait until a crisis to have these conversations with our parents?

The holidays are just around the corner. A new inflation report just dropped. That means one thing: the Cost of Thanksgiving Discourse. The most expensive part of Thanksgiving is now less about the table and more about how you get there.

Even physicians who often have a 403(b), 457(b), or defined benefit plan available too, usually max out their 401(k) first. The 401(k) is the best retirement account most workers can get, and that it’s still worth it for doctors.

That habit got expensive in 2026. Itemizers now lose the deduction on the first 0.5% of AGI they give away, and top-bracket donors see the tax benefit capped at 35%. The write-off shrinks unless you change how the money leaves your account before December 31.

The 2026 tax rules changed how charitable gifts are deducted. Join Earned and Physician on FIRE to learn what changed, how to give more tax-efficiently, and what to do before year-end.

Give appreciated stock in place of cash and the capital gain never shows up on your return. Bunch two or three years of donations into a donor-advised fund and you clear the floor once. Past 70½? Send the gift straight from your IRA.

Which move fits depends on whether you’ll itemize this year.

#8503. 7 Things Stranger Things Taught Me About Saving My Retirement From the IRS

Stranger Things Day slipped past earlier this month. Fans mark it every November 6, the anniversary of the night in 1983 when Will Byers rode his bike home from Mike’s basement and never made it.

One minute he was pedaling through Hawkins, Indiana, and the next he was gone, swallowed by a dimension running parallel to his own. Same streets, same house, just darker, colder, and coated in a black rot that fed on everything it touched.

If you missed the rewatch and the Eggo waffles, you have 354 days until the next one. You have 44 until December 31.

Your retirement savings took the same trip Will did. Nobody stole the money. It got relocated. The IRS built a gate decades ago, and your 401(k), your IRA, and your SEP all got pulled through it. The balance shows up in your statement. Touching it before 59½ costs a ransom.

By the time Stranger Things Day rolls around again on November 6, 2027, the 2026 tax year will be closed and filed. Every move in this article that opens an exit, the conversions, the contributions, the rollovers you make or wisely skip, has to happen before the ball drops on New Year’s Eve. The IRS doesn’t hand out extensions on the calendar.

Stranger Things needed five seasons to explain the Upside Down: what it was, how it touched the real world, where the gates opened and closed. Viewers watched the characters stumble through it for years with Christmas lights and homemade gear because no one who understood the place ever sat them down and drew it out.

That is the average physician’s relationship with the tax code.

Thousands of pages, scattered across decades of amendments and rulings and bills with names like SECURE Act 2.0 and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

Medical school skips it. Residency skips it too. And the advisor managing your portfolio, assuming you have one, probably maxed your employer 401(k), mentioned a backdoor Roth in passing, and called it a day.

The exits are sitting right there in the code, seven of them, penalty-free and legal, like the hidden passages in the Creel house. Physicians retire years later than they want to, or burn out before they get there, because nobody drew them the map.

This is the map, updated for 2026, a year when the rules changed in your favor for once.

Season one gave us the Demogorgon, a faceless predator that dragged people into the Upside Down and fed on them. The whole town lived in fear of a thing it didn’t understand.

The 10% early withdrawal penalty is the Demogorgon.

The 2026 tax rules changed how charitable gifts are deducted. Join Earned and Physician on FIRE to learn what changed, how to give more tax-efficiently, and what to do before year-end.

Featuring Carole Foos, CPA, Managing Director at Earned, and Jorge Sanchez, MD, of Physician on FIRE.

Takeaway: A practical year-end giving checklist to help you act before December 31.

Tue, Nov 17  ·  2:30 pm ET  ·  11:30 am PT

Pull money from an IRA or 401(k) before 59½ and the IRS adds 10% on top of ordinary income tax. For a physician in a high bracket, the combined hit can eat close to half of whatever comes out.

The Demogorgon doesn’t negotiate. Burned out at 57, practice imploded, three kids in college and a cash crunch right now? It takes its cut regardless.

What the residents of Hawkins never learned was that the monster had weaknesses. Enough heat and it retreated. Eleven could stop it cold. The penalty has weaknesses too, seven of them, and the rest of this piece walks through each one.

Eleven could move objects, close gates, and stop the worst things the Upside Down produced. She’d spent years locked in a government lab, and most people had no idea she existed.

The assumption bleeding W-2 physicians dry is that a Solo 401(k) belongs only to private practice owners and full-time contractors. Any physician with self-employment income and no full-time employees qualifies.

The hospitalist picking up two weekend locum shifts a month qualifies, as does the employed cardiologist who took a single paid speaking gig and the academic who cashed a CME honorarium check.

The size of that income sets how much you can contribute. It never decides whether you’re eligible.

For 2026, total contributions to a Solo 401(k) cap out at $72,000 per person. Inside that structure lives the Mega Backdoor Roth: after-tax contributions to the Solo 401(k), converted to Roth either in-plan or by rolling them out to a Roth IRA.

A tax-free bucket that grows without the government touching the back end, with contribution basis you can reach when you need it.

You and your spouse both work in a practice with no other full-time employees? Each of you can put in up to $72,000, which means $144,000 a year flowing into Roth. Let that run five years and you’re sitting on a pool of penalty-free basis the IRS has no further claim on.

The 2026 wrinkle that tilts the math further: under SECURE Act 2.0, anyone who earned more than $150,000 in FICA wages from an employer last year and makes catch-up contributions to that employer’s plan must now make them as Roth.

The pre-tax catch-up option is gone for high earners. The government forced your hand on $8,000 of after-tax money. The Solo 401(k) lets you do the same thing deliberately, at scale, with $72,000.

Most physicians never open one because most content written for physicians stops at the employer 401(k). Setting one up takes an afternoon. Leaving it unopened while the income to fund it is already landing in your checking account is an information problem, and information problems are cheap to fix.

Season two introduced the Mind Flayer, a massive psychic entity that didn’t kill its victims outright. It possessed them. Its hosts acted against their own interests, convinced the whole time they were doing the right thing.

Physicians who botch the backdoor Roth rarely make obvious errors. The pro-rata rule has possessed them, and they don’t know it.

The backdoor Roth, done right: make a non-deductible contribution to a Traditional IRA ($7,500 in 2026, $8,600 if you’re 50 or older).

Confirm you hold zero pre-tax IRA dollars anywhere under your name, meaning no SEP-IRA, no rollover IRA, no forgotten traditional IRA from residency parked at a custodian you haven’t logged into since 2015. Convert. No income limit, no penalty.

The pro-rata rule wrecks the whole thing the moment pre-tax IRA dollars enter the picture. The IRS won’t let you convert only the after-tax portion. It blends every IRA you own into one pot and taxes the conversion proportionally. One forgotten pre-tax account turns a clean transaction into a partial tax event.

Career transitions are where physicians get exposed. Leaving academics and rolling the 403(b) into a rollover IRA.

Switching from group practice to 1099 work and parking the old 401(k) “temporarily.” Starting a new employed role months before the new plan opens its doors. Each one plants a pre-tax IRA landmine that quietly breaks the backdoor Roth for years.

The fix is to roll every pre-tax IRA dollar into the Solo 401(k) before running any backdoor conversion. The Solo 401(k) accepts incoming rollovers and clears the pro-rata calculation entirely. Close the gate before the Mind Flayer gets through, and the rest of the plan stays intact.

Season three ended on what felt like a win. The gate closed, Billy sacrificed himself, Hopper appeared to die, and Hawkins seemed to heal. Then season four arrived and Vecna had been working the whole time, building and feeding while everyone celebrated.

Physician burnout runs on the same script. Roughly half of physicians report burnout in Medscape’s annual surveys, which makes it less a risk factor than a coin flip. We acknowledge it at conferences, tape mental health flyers to the break room wall, and go back to the 60-hour weeks we call resilience.

A financial plan that only works if you never burn out is a prayer dressed up as a spreadsheet.

Enter the Rule of 55, one of the most useful provisions most physicians have never heard of. Separate from your employer (quit, retire, get laid off) during or after the calendar year you turn 55, and you can tap that employer’s 401(k) with no 10% penalty. Income tax still applies. The Demogorgon, though, is gone.

Dr. Addams burns out at 56. Dr. Smart at 57. Both qualify, provided they left the employer 401(k) alone.

That proviso is where the plan dies. Roll the 401(k) into an IRA before you separate and the Rule of 55 no longer applies, because the provision covers employer-sponsored plans only. Once the rollover clears, the window shuts for good.

A second move widens the window. Old 401(k) balances from prior employers that now sit in rollover IRAs can be consolidated into your current employer’s plan before you separate. Leave at 55 or later and the Rule of 55 covers the entire consolidated balance.

Some plans refuse incoming rollovers, so check with the administrator. For a physician who has collected balances across three hospitals and two practices, this can multiply the penalty-free pool available the day they decide they’re done.

If you’re in your early 50s and have so much as daydreamed about an early exit, stop rolling employer 401(k)s into IRAs. Leave them where they sit. You’re protecting an option.

Season four revealed that the Upside Down had a full tunnel network connecting distant points across Hawkins. It had existed all along. The kids who survived did so partly because they found the tunnels early enough to use them.

The Roth conversion ladder is the tunnel system.

In any low-income year, meaning any year your taxable income sits well below normal physician earnings, convert a chunk of pre-tax retirement money (Traditional IRA, SEP-IRA, Solo 401(k)) to a Roth IRA. Pay income tax on the converted amount at that year’s rate.

Five years from January 1 of the conversion year, those dollars become accessible penalty-free, regardless of your age.

2026 is an unusually good year to run conversions. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act made the lower TCJA brackets permanent and locked in the 20% pass-through deduction for physicians with 1099 income. Conversions done at today’s rates cost less than they would have under the old sunset schedule, and Congress rarely improves things twice in a row.

Each conversion year runs its own five-year clock. Convert in 2026 and those dollars open January 1, 2031. Convert again in 2027 and that tranche opens January 1, 2032. Run conversions every year and you build a rolling pipeline, a new tranche unlocking every January.

The years physicians routinely waste: the sabbatical between positions (a six-month gap is one of the most valuable tax-planning windows of an entire career), parental leave with no 1099 income, the ramp-up after joining a new practice, the W-2 to 1099 switch, the wind-down to part-time locums before full retirement.

Size each conversion to fill the 22% or 24% bracket without tripping IRMAA surcharges on Medicare premiums. The tragedy is the physician who takes six months off, earns half a year’s income, files a clean return, and converts nothing. Five figures of lifetime tax savings, gone.

Ted Weschler’s story makes the point. One of Warren Buffett’s deputies at Berkshire Hathaway built a Traditional IRA worth north of $100 million, then converted the entire thing to Roth and paid a reported $28 million in tax to do it.

Every dollar in that account now grows and distributes tax-free. The mechanics are identical whether you’re converting $50,000 or $50 million.

In season three, the Russians ran a secret facility beneath Starcourt Mall, funded and staffed outside every rule the people upstairs lived by.

The Solo 401(k) participant loan is your private underground operation.

Borrow up to $50,000 or 50% of the account balance, whichever is less, at any time and for any reason. There’s no credit check or underwriter, and no waiting period. You approve your own loan. The rate runs around prime, and every dollar of interest flows back into your own account, so you’re paying yourself.

The physician use cases are specific: a down payment on a rental property during a cash-lean year, bridge funding during a practice startup before revenue normalizes, or covering a surprise expense without selling appreciated holdings in a taxable account and triggering capital gains.

Employer 401(k) loans carry a risk the Solo 401(k) deletes. Leave your job with an outstanding employer loan and the full balance comes due by your tax filing deadline; fail to repay and the IRS reclassifies it as a distribution, taxable plus the 10% penalty. You cannot fire yourself from your own plan. That risk doesn’t exist here.

The series finale didn’t end through brute force. It ended because the characters finally understood the rules of the dimension well enough to find exits nobody had used.

SECURE Act 2.0 added penalty exceptions that read, with only slight exaggeration, like admission criteria. Physicians should recognize them on sight. Few have seen them applied to their own accounts.

The terminal illness provision stops physicians cold the first time they hear it. If a physician certifies that a patient’s condition is expected to result in death within 84 months, that patient can tap any retirement account penalty-free, with optional repayment within three years if the patient recovers. You write this certification regularly. It applies to your own accounts in exactly the same way, and almost no one knows it.

The claim that retirement accounts lock money away is far less true than it was five years ago. These accounts now double as a safety net. A physician who dismisses them as untouchable before 59½ is running on stale data.

In the finale, Hopper and Murray prepared to detonate a bomb to destroy the machine opening the gate. Bluntest instrument available, and at that moment, exactly the right tool.

IRS Rule 72(t) is a bomb. Understand what you’re detonating before you light the fuse.

Under 72(t), you commit to Substantially Equal Periodic Payments (SEPP) from your IRA or 401(k), penalty-free at any age, for the longer of five years or until you turn 59½. Start at 40 and you’re locked in for nearly two decades. Start at 57 and you serve five years.

Three calculation methods exist: Required Minimum Distribution (smallest payments, recalculated annually), Fixed Amortization (highest payments, fixed), and Fixed Annuitization (similar to amortization, also fixed). Most people pick fixed amortization.

The 2026 tax rules changed how charitable gifts are deducted. Join Earned and Physician on FIRE to learn what changed, how to give more tax-efficiently, and what to do before year-end.

Featuring Carole Foos, CPA, Managing Director at Earned, and Jorge Sanchez, MD, of Physician on FIRE.

Takeaway: A practical year-end giving checklist to help you act before December 31.

Tue, Nov 17  ·  2:30 pm ET  ·  11:30 am PT

The catch is severe. Break the schedule in any way, a missed payment, a modification, a single deviation, and the IRS retroactively applies the 10% penalty to every distribution already taken, plus interest. Seven years into a schedule, that bill can be devastating.

One structural move contains the damage. Before starting, split the IRA into two accounts. Apply 72(t) only to the smaller one, sized to produce exactly the income you need, and leave the larger account untouched. An error then costs you the small account’s history, while the bulk of your savings keeps compounding.

72(t) fits the physician who retires well before 55 with a large IRA and needs predictable income before the Roth ladder finishes building. Right tool for a narrow situation, and a poor first resort.

Good diagnosticians don’t commit to one diagnosis before ruling out the alternatives. They build a differential and sequence the workup around probability, available data, and the patient in front of them.

These seven strategies work the same way. No single provision fits every physician, and the right sequence depends on age, income type, career stage, and how close the exit door really is.

Any age, any 1099 income at all: open a Solo 401(k) and max the Mega Backdoor Roth at $72,000. Over 50 and high-earning? Your catch-up contributions have to be Roth anyway, so lean in at scale.

Any low-income year, whether sabbatical, parental leave, practice transition, or a W-2 to 1099 switch: run a Roth conversion. The OBBBA rate environment favors you. Fill the lower brackets and start the five-year clock.

Early 50s and still employed somewhere: stop rolling old 401(k)s into IRAs. Consolidate into the current employer plan and protect the Rule of 55 window.

55 or older and separating from an employer: tap the 401(k) under the Rule of 55 before considering any rollover. That window, once lost, does not reopen.

Pre-55 retirement with a large IRA: the Roth conversion ladder is the primary engine, with 72(t) as backup if the ladder can’t bridge the early years.

Any career stage: learn the SECURE Act 2.0 exceptions. Terminal illness certification, disability, unreimbursed medical expenses. The provisions exist, they’re legal, and they apply to you. Read them before you need them.

The most unsettling reveal in Stranger Things wasn’t the Mind Flayer or the Demogorgon or the Russians under the mall. It was Vecna, one entity pulling strings from the beginning, before anyone knew there were strings.

By the time the kids understood what they were up against, years had passed, and some of them never fully recovered.

Dr. Addams didn’t fail because he earned too little. He failed because no one showed him the exits, and by the time he needed one it was too late to build it. His plan was designed for Dr. Lucky, the physician who never burns out, earns steadily into his mid-60s, and retires on schedule into a fully funded life. Dr. Lucky is a statistical outlier. Dr. Addams and Dr. Smart are the population.

The tax code wasn’t written with physicians in mind, and it doesn’t discriminate against them either. The rules work the same whether you trained at a top academic center or a community program, whether you’re W-2 or 1099, whether you’re planning an exit in three years or still convinced you’ll never burn out.

Right now, in November 2026, you have time. The 2026 tax year is still open. Conversions completed before December 31 start a clock that opens January 1, 2031. Solo 401(k) contributions for 2026 can be made up to your business tax filing deadline. The IRS is expected to announce 2027 limits any day now, with Milliman and Mercer both projecting $25,500 for 401(k) deferrals and $75,000 for total Solo 401(k) contributions. More room to build.

April 15, 2027 arrives the same way every year. The gate doesn’t wait for you to feel ready.

The physicians who retire on their own timeline read the map before they needed it. They found Eleven, ran conversions during the low-income years everyone else treated as inconveniences, stopped rolling accounts into IRAs at 52, and walked out of their last job with options.

The Upside Down has exits. All seven have been there the whole time.

Friends don’t let friends pay the early withdrawal penalty.

Jorge Sanchez, MD is the co-owner of Physician on Fire. This article is for informational and educational purposes only and does not constitute personalized tax, legal, or investment advice. Consult a qualified financial professional before implementing any retirement planning strategy. Contribution limits reflect confirmed 2026 IRS figures; 2027 figures are projections pending the official IRS announcement.

Your December Check-Writing Ritual Needs an Upgrade

Most physicians give the same way every year: a few checks go out after Christmas, and the CPA sorts it out in March.

That habit got expensive in 2026. Itemizers now lose the deduction on the first 0.5% of AGI they give away, and top-bracket donors see the tax benefit capped at 35%. The write-off shrinks unless you change how the money leaves your account before December 31.

Give appreciated stock in place of cash and the capital gain never shows up on your return. Bunch two or three years of donations into a donor-advised fund and you clear the floor once. Past 70½? Send the gift straight from your IRA.

Which move fits depends on whether you’ll itemize this year.

#8502. Crew Review: High-Yield Checking With Built-In Budgeting for Families

Managing money as a household is harder than it looks. Most people use a regular checking account at a big bank, then juggle a separate budgeting app, maybe a savings account somewhere else, and possibly a kids’ debit card on top of that. It’s a lot to keep track of.

Crew is a fintech app that tries to put all of that in one place. It combines a high-yield checking account, built-in budgeting tools, and family banking features – all inside a single app. The goal is to help you organize your money, automate your budget, and earn more interest without switching between apps.

In this Crew review, we cover what it is, how it works, who it’s best for, the key features, pricing, and what real users are saying. If you’re looking for a smarter checking account that does more, this review gives you the full picture.

Crew is a fintech app that tries to put all of that in one place. It combines a high-yield checking account, built-in budgeting tools, and family banking features

• High-yield checking • Debit cards available for kids• Unlimited budgeting pockets• Cash deposits and mobile check deposit• No monthly fees or minimum balances

• App-only banking with no desktop login• No physical check writing

Crew is a financial technology (fintech) company based in Lehi, Utah. It was founded by Gentry Davies and Steve Domino, who previously worked at Divvy, a business expense platform acquired by Bill.com. The app launched publicly and has been growing steadily since 2023.

Crew is not a bank. Banking services are provided by Bangor Savings Bank, which is FDIC-insured. Your deposits are held at Bangor Savings Bank, so they are protected up to federal insurance limits – $250,000 for individual accounts and $500,000 for joint accounts.

The app is available on both iOS and Android. A web app is currently in beta.

Crew works well for a wide range of people, but it’s especially useful if you fall into one of these groups:

Crew offers a checking account that earns 2.95% APY on your full balance. This rate applies to every dollar you hold in the account – there’s no minimum deposit requirement and no tiered rate structure.

Why it matters: Most big bank checking accounts pay close to 0.01% APY. Earning nearly 3% on your everyday checking balance can add meaningful interest over time, especially for families keeping a few thousand dollars in their account at any given time.

Pockets are virtual “buckets” inside your single Crew checking account. You can create as many as you need – for example, one for bills, one for savings, one for a vacation fund, one for groceries.

Why it matters: You don’t need a separate savings account or multiple bank accounts. Pockets let you visually and mentally divide your money without moving it to another institution. You can also lock a pocket in “piggy bank mode” to avoid dipping into it.

Crew’s Autopilot feature lets you create rules that move money automatically based on triggers. Triggers can be events like a paycheck arriving or a balance dropping below a set level, or they can be time-based, like every Friday or the 1st of the month.

Why it matters: Automation removes the discipline requirement from budgeting. You set your rules once, and Crew handles the rest. For example, you can tell Crew to automatically send 10% of every paycheck to your giving pocket, $500 to bills, and keep the rest in checking — without touching the app every payday.

Crew supports joint accounts for couples and child accounts for kids. Each child gets their own Crew account with a debit card that has their name on it. Kids can log into the app with their own login to check their balance and track spending.

Why it matters: Most banking apps bolt on a kid’s account as an afterthought. Crew builds family banking into the core experience. Parents get real-time spending notifications, spend controls, and the ability to set automated allowances.

Parents can set up automatic recurring transfers to a child’s account. You define the amount and the schedule, and Crew handles the delivery.

Why it matters: Automated allowances teach kids about money while removing the “I forgot to pay your allowance” problem for parents. Kids learn what consistent saving looks like in practice.

Every account member gets a Mastercard debit card. You can switch which pocket your card draws from at any time inside the app – or update a transaction after the fact if you accidentally spent from the wrong pocket.

Why it matters: This setup means budgeting is “baked in” to your spending. Instead of tracking what you spent after the fact, you decide which budget category you’re spending from before or at the time of purchase.

You can use your Crew Mastercard at any ATM in the Mastercard, Maestro, or Cirrus networks. Crew does not have its own fee-free ATM network, but it reimburses ATM fees for up to 20 withdrawals per year.

Why it matters: The annual ATM fee reimbursement covers most casual cash users without adding much complexity.

Crew supports outgoing wire transfers. The fee depends on your total account balance.

Incoming wires and standard ACH transfers are processed as usual through the app.

Deposits held through Crew are insured through Bangor Savings Bank, a Member FDIC institution.

This is standard FDIC pass-through insurance. Crew’s website states that pass-through insurance is subject to certain conditions set forth in the deposit agreement.

Crew includes an AI-powered financial assistant called Penny. Penny can answer questions about your account, help you set up automations, and give you guidance on your financial situation.

Why it matters: Penny gives users a simple way to interact with their finances through natural language, without digging through menus.

One of Crew’s stronger selling points is its simple, low-fee structure. Here’s a clear breakdown:

Note: APY is variable and may change at any time. The 2.95% rate is the most recent published rate. Always check trycrew.com for the current rate before opening an account.

Opening a Crew account is quick. Most people complete it in under two minutes. Here are the steps:

To add a family member, go to the Family section of the app and follow the prompts to add a joint owner or create a child account.

No. Crew is a financial technology company, not a bank. Banking services are provided by Bangor Savings Bank, Member FDIC, which is a real, federally insured bank. Your deposits are held at Bangor Savings Bank, so they are FDIC insured up to federal limits.

The APY is variable, meaning it can change over time. It is not a limited-time promotional rate in the traditional sense; it applies to your full balance, with no minimum or expiration. However, Crew can adjust the rate when market conditions change. The rate has fluctuated over the app’s history (it was as high as 3.7% in early 2025). Referral sign-ups may qualify for a 0.5% APY boost for the first three months.

Cash deposit support has been in development. Some reviews noted it was not yet available at the time of writing, though the feature has been in the works. It’s worth checking the current app version or Crew’s website for the latest on cash deposits before signing up if this is important to you.

You need your legal name, date of birth, physical address, and a tax ID (typically your Social Security number). Most applicants complete the process in under two minutes.

Crew earns revenue in two ways: from the interest it earns on deposits held at Bangor Savings Bank, and from merchant fees when you use your Crew debit card to make purchases. This model is common among fintech companies and allows them to offer no-fee accounts while still generating revenue.

User feedback for Crew is largely positive, particularly among families and people who value built-in budgeting features.

Rating: 4.8 out of 5 stars (based on 179 reviews as of March 2026)

Positive trends from Google Play users include:

Crew’s iOS app carries consistently high ratings. Users describe it as well-designed and easy to navigate. Family features are frequently praised, with parents noting that kids enjoy having their own card and app login.

Reviewers across platforms repeatedly mention Crew as a genuine alternative to maintaining separate banking and budgeting apps. The combination of high-yield checking, automatic paycheck splitting, and child accounts in one place is the most-cited reason for switching from other banks or apps.

The most consistent piece of constructive feedback is that Crew is still a young product and some features – like the web app – are still catching up to the mobile experience.

Crew is a well-designed fintech product that combines several things that usually require multiple apps or accounts: a high-yield checking account, budgeting through pockets, spending automation, and family banking.

Overall, Crew fills a genuine gap. Most checking accounts don’t pay meaningful interest and don’t have built-in budgeting. Crew does both, and it adds family banking on top. For households looking to simplify their financial toolkit and earn more interest on everyday balances, it’s worth a serious look.

As always, make sure to read the deposit agreement and check the current APY at trycrew.com before opening an account, since rates are variable and can change.

This review is for informational purposes only and does not constitute financial advice. APY rates, fees, and features are subject to change. Always verify current terms directly with Crew at trycrew.com before making any financial decisions.

#8501. Aeroplan Stopovers — Two Cities for the Price of One

One of the highest-value redemptions in travel rewards

Picture this: you're settling into a lie-flat business class seat somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of something cold in hand, knowing that in 48 hours you'll be waking up in Istanbul — and then, a few days later, continuing onward to Bangkok. Two bucket-list cities. One award booking. One points balance. This is what the Aeroplan stopover sweet spot feels like in practice. It's not a trick or a loophole — it's a deliberately designed feature of Air Canada's Aeroplan program that the vast majority of travelers simply don't know exists. And that gap between awareness and reality is exactly where the ChooseFI community finds its edge. Here's the math that should make your jaw drop. A business class itinerary from North America to Istanbul with a continuing flight onward to Bangkok — two long-haul segments, lie-flat seats, Star Alliance lounges at every connection — would cost somewhere between **$6,000 and $15,000 in cash**. That's a realistic retail range depending on season and how far out you book. Most people never consider it a possibility for a family vacation or a milestone trip because the sticker price puts it in a different universe. With Aeroplan, you're booking that same itinerary — the same seats, the same lounges, the same Turkish Airlines or Thai Airways product — for **75,000 Aeroplan points**. At the low end of the cash price range, that's already **8 cents per point**. At the high end, you're extracting **20 cents per point** from a currency that most people earned by putting groceries on a credit card. The pricing inefficiency here is structural. Aeroplan's partner award chart prices long-haul business class at a fixed rate regardless of cash fare fluctuations. When business class prices spike — around holidays, during peak travel seasons, during major events — your points cost stays exactly the same. You're insulated from the market. That's the FI mindset applied to travel: you've already paid for the trip in points, slowly accumulated through everyday spending, and now you're simply redeeming the stored value. The stopover itself is nearly free. Aeroplan charges just 5,000 extra miles to add a stopover city to a one-way award. That means your Istanbul layover becomes a multi-day stay — at zero additional points cost beyond that small add-on — and you haven't booked a second award at all. One booking. Two destinations. That's the entire premise, and once you see it, you can't unsee it.

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegantly simple once you understand it, but it requires knowing three things that most travelers don't: how Aeroplan's routing rules work, what a stopover actually is in the context of an award ticket, and why Star Alliance's global network makes this scalable to almost any destination pair you can imagine.

When Aeroplan relaunched its loyalty program in 2020, it did something remarkable: it eliminated fuel surcharges entirely and published a partner award chart with fixed pricing for flights on Star Alliance carriers. This is critical. When you book Turkish Airlines business class through Aeroplan, you pay the Aeroplan fixed chart rate — not what Turkish Airlines would charge in its own currency or miles program, and not the inflated cash price. That fixed chart is the engine of this redemption.

For long-haul international business class, Aeroplan's chart prices routing through multiple regions based on your origin and destination — not every intermediate stop. This is the aha moment. Aeroplan determines your award price based on where your journey starts and where it ends, and then allows you to add a stopover in between for just 5,000 additional miles. The stopover city is priced as a pass-through for the purpose of calculating your award zone, not as a second trip.

On a one-way Aeroplan award, you're permitted to add a free stopover — meaning you can stay in an intermediate city for any length of time before continuing to your final destination. That 5,000-mile add-on is essentially the cost of a full additional destination. Compare that to booking a second one-way award from Istanbul to Bangkok, which would cost you another 40,000–55,000 Aeroplan points in business class. The math is decisive.

The routing must be geographically sensible — you can't fly backwards across the globe — but Aeroplan's allowance for multi-segment itineraries through Star Alliance hubs gives you enormous flexibility. Istanbul (IST) is a Turkish Airlines hub. Bangkok (BKK) is served by Thai Airways and several Star Alliance carriers. Both are Star Alliance partners. Both are bookable through Aeroplan at fixed chart rates with no fuel surcharges.

The best part for the ChooseFI community is how accessible the underlying points are. Aeroplan accepts transfers from four major programs:

Chase's instant transfer speed is particularly valuable here. When you find business class availability — which can disappear quickly — you want to move points immediately. Having Chase Ultimate Rewards as your primary earning currency means you can search, find space, and transfer points before the availability window closes. The 1:1 ratio across all four programs means no conversion math — every point you earn translates directly to one Aeroplan mile.

Booking an Aeroplan stopover award in business class is genuinely one of the more complex redemptions in the travel rewards world, but it becomes manageable when you break it into distinct phases. Here's exactly how to do it.

Start by deciding on your two destinations. Aeroplan stopovers work best when your intermediate city is a major Star Alliance hub that lies geographically between your origin and final destination. Classic combinations include North America to Istanbul (Turkish Airlines hub) continuing to Southeast Asia, or North America to a European hub continuing to the Middle East or East Africa. Your stopover city should be somewhere you genuinely want to spend 2–5 days — this is a real trip, not just a layover.

This is the most important and most time-consuming step. You need to find saver-level business class availability on both segments independently before you book.

Once you've confirmed availability on both segments, go to aeroplan.com and use the multi-city search function. Enter your full itinerary — origin, stopover city with your intended layover dates, and final destination.

Once you've confirmed the award is bookable and are ready to complete the reservation:

Complete your booking on aeroplan.com or with a phone agent, confirm the stopover is properly reflected in your itinerary, and save every confirmation email. Verify your seats on each carrier's website immediately after booking.

A stopover is an intentional break in your journey lasting more than 24 hours at a connecting city. Most airlines treat stopovers as separate tickets, charging full price for each segment. Aeroplan is one of the few programs that allows a free stopover on round-trip awards, letting you explore a connecting city for days before continuing to your final destination. This is fundamentally different from a layover, which is a brief connection of a few hours at an airport. The stopover must be in a city served by a Star Alliance carrier on your routing, and the key is that Aeroplan prices the entire itinerary as one award, not two.

Card links may earn ChooseFI a commission. See our advertiser disclosure.

Let's build a real example so you can see exactly what this looks like on paper — and in the air.

The Route: Toronto (YYZ) → Istanbul (IST, 4-day stopover) → Bangkok (BKK) The Carrier: Turkish Airlines business class on both segments The Points Cost: 75,000 Aeroplan miles for the two segments + 5,000 miles for the stopover = 80,000 Aeroplan miles total Cash Equivalent: A comparable business class itinerary on this routing typically retails for $9,000–$12,000 in 2026, depending on when you search and how far in advance you book.

The CPP Calculation: At the midpoint cash value of $10,500 against 80,000 points, you're extracting 13.1 cents per Aeroplan mile — well inside the 8–20 cent range this sweet spot delivers, and roughly 10–13 times the value of redeeming Aeroplan miles for cash back.

The Turkish Airlines business class product on long-haul routes is consistently rated among the top business class experiences in the Star Alliance network. On the YYZ–IST segment — operated on a 787 or A330 — you'll have access to a lie-flat seat with direct aisle access, the Turkish Airlines Lounge in Istanbul (widely considered one of the best airport lounges in the world, full stop), and a meal service that reflects the airline's culinary reputation. The IST lounge alone — with its restaurant, spa, golf simulator, and sleeping areas — is worth lingering in even before your onward connection.

In Istanbul, your four days might include the Hagia Sophia at sunrise, a Bosphorus dinner cruise, and the Grand Bazaar before you head to the airport to continue your journey. You've paid nothing additional for this stay beyond the 5,000-mile stopover fee.

The IST–BKK segment puts you into Bangkok in the evening, ready for Thailand's extraordinary food, culture, and cost of living — which, for the FI-minded traveler, means your lodging and meals on the ground are remarkably affordable, stretching the value of your trip even further.

Total points cost for two lie-flat business class segments and a full European city stay: 80,000 miles, earned on everyday credit card spending. That's the entire proposition, and those numbers are real.

Book at exactly 355 days out. Aeroplan opens its booking window at 355 days before departure. The best business class availability on popular routes — especially Turkish Airlines long-haul — appears at this window and gets claimed quickly. Set a calendar reminder and be ready to search at the 355-day mark for your target travel dates.

Use Chase Ultimate Rewards as your primary earning currency for this redemption. The instant transfer speed to Aeroplan is genuinely differentiating. When you find award space and need to move quickly, Chase lets you transfer and book in the same session. Amex, Capital One, and Bilt all require 1–2 days, during which your availability can evaporate.

Search availability before you transfer points. Confirm space exists on every segment before a single point moves. There's no undo button on a transfer, and Aeroplan points sitting idle in your account are fine — points transferred to an account where you can't find availability are a headache.

Call Aeroplan for complex routings. The online multi-city tool is functional but can struggle with nuanced stopover configurations. Phone agents are experienced with these bookings and have the same access to inventory. The call is worth it for an $80,000-point booking.

Leverage the open-jaw rule too. Aeroplan also allows open-jaw routing — fly into one city, depart from another. Combined with the stopover, you can design a route that visits three geographic points on a single award: fly into Istanbul, take trains or ferries to Athens, and fly home from Athens. The award prices the same way.

Don't assume partner availability matches Aeroplan's search. Turkish Airlines and other Star Alliance partners don't always make every seat available through Aeroplan's online portal. If you see space on the carrier's own site but not on aeroplan.com, call — agents can often access inventory the website misses.

Don't book inflexible connecting flights. Long-haul itineraries with tight connections are a risk. Build in at least a 3-hour connection at hub airports to protect against irregular operations that could affect your award segments.

Don't earn Marriott Bonvoy® points with this redemption in mind. The 3:1 transfer ratio to Aeroplan makes Marriott a poor choice for funding this specific award. Stick to Amex, Chase, Capital One, or Bilt at 1:1.

Don't book this for a time-sensitive trip. Award availability, transfer timelines, and multi-carrier coordination mean this requires planning runway. Build in at least 3–4 weeks of lead time beyond the actual booking date.

This redemption is purpose-built for the advanced travel rewards enthusiast in the ChooseFI community — someone who has already mastered the basics (earning transferable points, understanding award charts, booking straightforward partner awards) and is ready to unlock the next level of value.

The ideal profile: A couple or solo traveler planning a milestone trip — a significant anniversary, a sabbatical, a once-in-a-decade adventure — who wants to experience two destinations in business class without paying business class prices for either one. You're flexible on travel dates, comfortable spending time on the phone with an airline agent, and genuinely excited about the trip-planning process as part of the experience.

Minimum points balance: You'll need approximately 80,000 Aeroplan miles to complete this booking (75,000 for the award plus 5,000 for the stopover). That's achievable from a single premium credit card welcome bonus, a combination of two or three mid-tier welcome bonuses, or 12–18 months of everyday spending on a 2x transferable points card.

For the ChooseFI traveler who's been building transferable points for a year or two and wants to see what this system is truly capable of, this redemption is the answer.

This redemption is rated **Hard** — and that rating is honest. It earns that designation from three compounding challenges, not just one. **Challenge 1: Finding availability on multiple segments simultaneously.** Business class award space on popular long-haul routes is limited. Finding saver-level availability on one segment is manageable. Finding it on two connected segments, with dates that create a coherent stopover itinerary, requires persistence and flexibility. This is the primary barrier. **Challenge 2: Understanding Aeroplan's routing logic.** Aeroplan's stopover rules, multi-city booking interface, and the distinction between how partner awards are priced require more than surface-level familiarity with the program. A misunderstanding of how the stopover is added can result in a significantly higher points cost or a booking that doesn't reflect your intended itinerary. **Challenge 3: Coordinating the transfer timing.** With a 355-day booking window and fast-moving business class availability, the timing of your point transfers requires active management — particularly if you're not using Chase's instant transfer speed. ## Three Tips to Overcome These Challenges 1. **Start your availability research 60–90 days before the 355-day window opens.** Know your target route, your preferred stopover city, and your date range before you ever log into aeroplan.com. Preparation turns a chaotic search into a focused one. 2. **Use united.com as your availability research tool.** It searches the Star Alliance network and shows you realistic inventory without requiring you to commit points. 3. **Don't be discouraged by the learning curve.** Every hard redemption in the ChooseFI community gets easier the second time. Plenty of members who now book these routinely considered them impossible the first time they looked. The complexity is real — but so is the $10,000 of value sitting on the other side of it.

Pick a final destination and a stopover city on the same Star Alliance routing. Classic combos: Istanbul + Bangkok, Zurich + Tokyo, Vienna + Singapore. The stopover city must be a natural connection point on a Star Alliance route between your origin and destination.

Set a calendar alert for 355 days before your departure date. Search for business class availability on each segment separately using United.com or Aeroplan.com. Both legs need saver-level award space on the same booking.

Before transferring any points, verify that saver award space exists on both the outbound leg (origin to stopover city) and the continuation (stopover city to final destination). If either segment is unavailable, the booking will not work.

Transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards (instant) or Amex Membership Rewards (1-2 days) to your Aeroplan account at a 1:1 ratio. Only transfer once you have confirmed availability on both segments.

Call Aeroplan or use the multi-city search tool online. Specify your stopover city and duration (up to the maximum allowed). The system prices it as one round-trip award. Confirm total points match expectations before completing the booking.

Aeroplan allows stopovers of up to 45 days on round-trip awards. You can stay in your stopover city for a few days or several weeks, giving you genuine time to explore rather than just passing through.

No, stopovers are only available on round-trip awards through Aeroplan. One-way bookings do not qualify for the free stopover benefit. This is one reason round-trip awards can offer better value than two one-ways.

Aeroplan has improved its online multi-city search tool, and some stopover itineraries can now be booked online. However, complex routings may still require a phone call. When calling, clearly state you want a round-trip award with a stopover and specify your stopover city and dates.

The best stopover cities are Star Alliance hub cities with strong business class availability: Istanbul (Turkish Airlines hub), Zurich (SWISS hub), Vienna (Austrian hub), Singapore (Singapore Airlines hub), and Tokyo (ANA hub). These hubs offer the most consistent saver-level award space.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

The Aeroplan stopover is one of the most powerful tools in the travel rewards playbook. By adding a free stopover to a round-trip business class award, you can explore two world-class cities for the points cost of visiting one. It requires planning, patience at the 355-day booking window, and comfort with Star Alliance routing rules, but the payoff is extraordinary: 10-15 cents per point in value on experiences that would cost thousands in cash. For the FI community member who has mastered basic award bookings and is ready to level up, this is the redemption that changes how you think about travel.

From its humble beginnings in 2008 to today, Bitcoin’s history has been relatively short but very eventful. The original protocol for this popular digital currency was created in 2008 by Satoshi Nakamoto, believed to be a pseudonym for an unknown developer or group of developers.

Nakamoto launched the Bitcoin network just a year later and began mining the currency— an estimated 1 million bitcoins were mined in the early years.

The creator(s) of this first-of-its-kind asset developed the cryptocurrency in response to the Great Recession of 2007-2009, spurred by a distrust of the traditional banking system and concerns about its stability.

Given the recent values of Bitcoin, it’s hard to believe the currency first started trading on exchanges in 2010 at under $0.10. Since then, it’s experienced astronomical growth and some pretty wild price swings.

At its most recent high, one bitcoin was worth over $64,000—a far cry from trading for pennies in its earliest days.

Whether you’re thinking of investing in Bitcoin or you’ve held this cryptocurrency for several years, it’s fun to look back at this groundbreaking asset’s history. Read on for insights on Bitcoin milestones, historical returns, and how its returns compare to those of other assets.

Since being created, Bitcoin has experienced several milestones. Here’s a look back at some of the most significant moments in the short history of this cryptocurrency:

While Bitcoin isn’t exempt from the volatility cryptocurrencies often experience, it’s delivered some impressive returns over the years. Here’s a look at Bitcoin’s annual returns from 2010 to 2022:

And here’s a look at monthly returns, if you feel like getting a deeper dive:

While Bitcoin has experienced some wild monthly price swings and a couple of years where its value has declined, you can see that its declines have been eclipsed by some incredible gains. Now let’s explore how Bitcoin’s value has changed over 10, 5, 3, and 1 years.

Let’s say you bought one bitcoin on August, 3rd 2013, for $1,106.75, its price at the time. If you held that one bitcoin until August 3rd, 2023, it would’ve been worth $29,310.44, and your total ROI for the 10 years would be 2,546.8%.

We’ll also assume you purchased one Bitcoin for this example. A single bitcoin was valued at $965.31 on August, 3rd, 2018, and its value climbed to $29,310.44 by August 2023. Using our calculation above, your total ROI for those five years would be 294.1%.

A single bitcoin was valued at $11,246.20 in August 2020, and its value climbed to $29,310.44 at the end of 2021. Your total ROI for those three years would be 160.6%.

If you purchased a single bitcoin in August 2022, you would’ve paid around $22,626.83. In one year, that value would’ve increased to $29,310.44. Your total returns for that year would be 29.54%.

Instead of buying one bitcoin, let’s say you decided to invest $1,000 into Bitcoin. Here’s a look at how this $1,000 investment would’ve performed if you bought and held your Bitcoin for 10, 5, 3, and 1 years.

While Bitcoin’s earliest investors would have benefitted the most from buying and holding their Bitcoin, those who’ve invested recently also fared well.

If you’re curious how Bitcoin returns compare to those of other asset classes, here’s how its annual and total returns compare to gold, real estate, and the S&P 500.(Spoiler alert: Bitcoin outperformed all three assets by an enormous margin.)

If you compare Bitcoin’s returns to gold’s returns, you’ll notice a stark difference. Bitcoin has an average annual return of 1,576% and a total return of 18,912% from 2010 to 2022, while SPDR Gold Shares had an average annual return of just 5.14% and a total return of 61.67% over the same period.

Let’s see if real estate fared any better compared to Bitcoin. The cryptocurrency delivered a whopping 1,576% average annual return and an 18,912% total return from 2010 to 2021, while the Vanguard Real Estate ETF had an average annual return of 13.49% and a total return of 161.91% over the same period.

So, real estate saw slightly higher returns than gold, but it still didn’t come close to Bitcoin’s returns.

The S&P 500 didn’t fare too much better in its head-to-head with Bitcoin. From 2011 to 2023, the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF delivered an average annual return of 15.74% and a total return of 173.14%. While those numbers aren’t too shabby, Bitcoin’s average annual return for the same period was a whopping 819%, and its total return was 9,012%.

We’ve analyzed how Bitcoin compares to gold, real estate, and the stock market, but how does it stack up against some of the best-performing stocks? Here’s how this popular cryptocurrency stacks up against major companies like Amazon, Apple, Berkshire Hathaway, JP Morgan, Microsoft, Visa, and Walmart.

We looked at the average annual and total returns for each asset. This data assumes you bought the asset in 2010 and held it until 2023.

While some investors may be skeptical about cryptocurrency, citing concerns over market volatility and a high risk of loss, Bitcoin’s performance over time paints a rosy picture. With its longevity and astronomically high returns, Bitcoin has been worth the risk for many investors—especially early adopters.

Of course, historical performance doesn’t guarantee future returns. So if you’re considering investing in cryptocurrency, only invest what you can afford to lose.

#8499. Debbie App: Can This App Really Help You Pay Off Debt Faster?

Debbie is a debt payoff app built around a truth most people already understand but rarely see addressed in finance tools: paying off debt is not just about numbers, it is about behavior. And if behavior is the real challenge, motivation matters more than spreadsheets.

Most personal finance apps track balances and interest rates and then stop there. Debbie goes a step further by rewarding people for making progress. When you do the right things consistently, you do not just see your debt go down. You actually get something back.

Many debt payoff journeys fail in the same place. Not at the beginning, when motivation is high, but in the middle, when progress feels slow, and life gets in the way. Debbie is designed specifically for that phase.

After connecting your credit cards, student loans, or other debts, the app creates a personalized payoff plan based on your balances and payment history. The plan is realistic and focused on consistency rather than extreme sacrifices.

As you make payments and reduce balances, Debbie rewards you for that progress.

• Cash rewards• Gift cards• Partner offers tied to financial milestones

These rewards are not meant to eliminate debt on their own. They exist to reinforce the habit of showing up and sticking with the plan.

Debbie gives users a clean dashboard showing:

This reduces the mental stress of juggling multiple accounts.

Unlike most personal finance apps, Debbie pays users for progress, which helps reinforce positive habits. Over $2,319,961.65 earned by people reaching their money goals.

This makes it beginner-friendly, even for people new to budgeting or debt payoff.

Debbie works best for people who need accountability and encouragement. If you already know what to do but struggle to stay consistent, this app fills an important gap.

• Rewards that reinforce good financial behavior• A clean, easy to understand interface• A focus on progress instead of perfection• Motivation during the hardest part of the journey

There are also a few limitations to keep in mind. Debbie is not a replacement for a full budgeting system, and the rewards alone will not move the needle if you are carrying very large balances. You still have to do the work. The app simply makes it easier to keep going.

You will also need to link your financial accounts, which is standard for most modern finance apps but worth noting.

Debbie is a strong fit for people who feel overwhelmed by debt, burned out on traditional budgeting apps, or frustrated that they are doing the right things but still don’t feel any momentum.

If you are already highly disciplined and managing everything with detailed spreadsheets, you may not need the additional reinforcement. For most people, though, motivation is the missing piece.

Yes. Debbie is a legitimate personal finance app built around a behavior-driven debt payoff model. While it won’t magically erase debt, it helps users stay engaged, which is often the biggest missing piece in successfully paying off debt.

If you’re exploring Debbie, there are several other financial wellness and money-saving apps worth considering. Each app offers a different approach to helping users improve their finances, build better habits, or earn rewards.

Acorns automatically invests your spare change by rounding up purchases to the nearest dollar. It’s designed for beginners who want a simple, hands-off way to start investing.

Rocket Money focuses on budgeting, subscription tracking, and lowering monthly bills. It can help users identify recurring charges and negotiate certain expenses on their behalf.

Qapital combines budgeting with automated savings goals. Users can create custom “rules” that move money into savings automatically based on spending habits or milestones.

YNAB is a budgeting app built around giving every dollar a purpose. It’s popular among people who want a more hands-on system for managing cash flow and paying off debt.

Paying off debt is rarely about knowledge. Most people already know what they should be doing. The real challenge is sticking with the plan month after month, even when progress feels slow.

Debbie helps solve that problem by rewarding progress, reinforcing positive habits, and making the journey feel less discouraging. It will not magically erase debt. But it can absolutely help you stay consistent long enough to change your financial life.

Practical advice to help you make money, save money and pay off debt, from a family that paid off $52,000 in 18 months.

Most of the tax decisions that matter for 2026 have to be made by December 31. After that, the year is closed, and the return you file in April mostly reports what already happened.

That’s especially true this year. Recent regulations have changed several rules that hit physicians directly, from how catch up contributions work to what a charitable gift is worth. Some habits that worked last year now cost more.

Below is a year end tax planning checklist built for physicians: the retirement and giving sections apply to almost everyone, and the practice section covers owners and anyone with 1099 income.

Work through what applies to you and bring the list to your tax team before the holidays take over December. Every year our tax team sees the same pattern: the plan was sound, but one deadline slipped past because you only hear from your CPA in April.

Start with these before you check any boxes:

The deferral limit for 401(k), 403(b), and governmental 457 plans is $24,500 for 2026. The catch up for those 50 and older is 8,000(11,250 if you turn 60 to 63 in 2026), and the IRA limit rose to $7,500 (IRS Notice 2025-67).

If you’re 50 or older and earned more than $150,000 in FICA wages from your employer in 2025, your 2026 catch up contributions must go in as Roth (IRC §414(v)(7); IRS Notice 2025-67).

The SALT cap is $40,400 for 2026, but it shrinks by 30 cents for every dollar of modified AGI above $505,000. It bottoms out at $10,000 around $606,333 of MAGI, which is where some physician households land (One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Pub. L. 119-21; IRC §164(b)(7)).

Itemizers can only deduct charitable gifts above 0.5% of AGI (OBBBA, Pub. L. 119-21; IRC §170(b)(1)(I)). If you’re in the 37% bracket, the tax benefit of your itemized deductions is limited to roughly 35 cents per dollar (OBBBA, Pub. L. 119-21; IRC §68).

The dependent care FSA exclusion rose from $5,000 to $7,500, or $3,750 if married filing separately (OBBBA, Pub. L. 119-21; IRC §129(a)(2)).

Employee deferrals to a 401(k) or 403(b) have to come out of a 2026 paycheck. Check your total so far this year, and raise your election for the last few pay periods if you’re short of $24,500.

If you also have a 457(b), it carries its own $24,500 limit on top of your 401(k) or 403(b).

457(b) plans at nonprofit hospitals and other tax exempt employers work differently. They are unfunded, so the money stays an asset of your employer and is exposed to its creditors if the employer runs into financial trouble.

Their distribution rules also differ, so read the plan terms before you defer more.

If you’re 50 or older, check that your plan moved your catch up to Roth if the new rule applies to you. If your plan has no Roth option, high earners can’t make catch up contributions at all in 2026.

Moonlighting, locums, expert witness work, and side practices can all fund a Solo 401(k). The catch is that the $24,500 employee deferral limit is per person, across every plan you participate in.

If you’ve already maxed your hospital 403(b), your Solo 401(k) is limited to the employer contribution, which is roughly 20% of net self employment earnings. If you don’t have a plan set up yet, ask your tax team now, because the deadlines for opening a plan and electing deferrals are different.

The pro rata rule looks at your pretax traditional, SEP, and SIMPLE IRA balances on December 31. A pretax balance sitting there at year end can make part of your backdoor Roth conversion taxable.

The usual fix is rolling those balances into an employer plan that accepts them, and finishing the rollover before December 31. This is one of the most common backdoor Roth problems we catch, usually an old rollover IRA from a prior job that nobody remembered.

A conversion counts in the year it’s completed, and it can’t be undone. Physician on FIRE has a thorough breakdown of when Roth conversions make the most sense, especially in the years between retirement and required distributions.

S-Corp owners have to run their reasonable W-2 salary through payroll by year end. Set it too low and it won’t hold up to the IRS.

Set it too high and you give back payroll tax savings, so true it up in the final payroll runs.

If your practice elected PTET, the payment has to leave the practice account by December 31 to be deducted on your 2026 return.

Wages paid to your children for work actually done in 2026 are deductible to the practice. Up to the 2026 standard deduction of $16,100 (Rev. Proc. 2025-32), your child owes no federal income tax on those wages, assuming they have no other income.

In a sole proprietorship, or a partnership owned only by the child’s parents, wages to children under 18 also skip Social Security and Medicare tax. Corporations don’t get that exemption. Keep timesheets and run the wages through payroll.

OBBBA permanently restored 100% bonus depreciation for property acquired after January 19, 2025, so qualifying equipment can be fully deducted in the year it’s placed in service (OBBBA, Pub. L. 119-21; IRC §168(k)).

Equipment, software, and vehicles only count for 2026 if they’re placed in service by December 31. Buying in late December and installing in January moves the deduction into 2027. We see it every January: equipment ordered before the holidays that didn’t get installed until after New Year’s.

If you own your practice through an S-Corp or another entity, home office, cell phone, and mileage costs reimbursed under a written accountable plan are deductible to the practice and tax-free to you. Process 2026 reimbursements before the year closes.

Sole proprietors don’t need an accountable plan, since they deduct these costs directly on Schedule C.

The 0.5% floor means that with $500,000 of AGI, you get no deduction for the first $2,500 of gifts (OBBBA, Pub. L. 119-21; IRC §170(b)(1)(I)). Add the roughly 35 cent limit for filers in the top bracket (IRC §68), and small annual gifts are worth less than they were.

Two year end tax planning moves work better under the new rules:

Bunch your giving. Concentrate several years of gifts into one year, often through a donor advised fund, so more of the total clears the floor.

Give appreciated shares instead of cash. Donating shares held more than a year generally avoids capital gains tax on the appreciation, and the gift still counts toward your deduction.

If you take the standard deduction, you can now deduct up to 1,000ofcashgifts(2,000 married filing jointly) without itemizing (OBBBA, Pub. L. 119-21; IRC §170(p)). It covers cash gifts to qualifying charities, but not gifts to donor advised funds or most private foundations.

The last 2026 estimated payment is due January 15, 2027. If your 2025 AGI was over $150,000, paying 110% of your 2025 tax through withholding and estimates protects you from an underpayment penalty (IRS Publication 505).

If you’re W-2 with outside income, you have an extra option. The IRS treats withholding as if it were paid evenly throughout the year, so raising your December withholding can cover a shortfall from earlier quarters.

Open enrollment is happening now at most employers. If you pay for child care, you can elect up to $7,500 for 2027, up from the old $5,000 limit.

Dr. Lee is a hypothetical hospitalist, age 52, married filing jointly, with $380,000 of W-2 salary and about $60,000 of 1099 income from moonlighting. Here’s how the checklist plays out for her:

Her 403(b) deferrals are on pace to reach $24,500 by her final paycheck. Her 2025 FICA wages were over $150,000, so her $8,000 catch up goes in as Roth.

Because her 403(b) used up her deferral limit, the Solo 401(k) on her moonlighting income takes only the employer contribution, roughly 20% of her net self employment earnings.

She has a $40,000 rollover IRA from a prior job. She moves it into her 403(b) before December 31 so the pro rata rule doesn’t make most of her backdoor Roth conversion taxable.

She usually gives $6,000 a year. With AGI around $400,000, the first $2,000 isn’t deductible. She bunches three years of gifts, $18,000, into a donor advised fund this December. She loses the $2,000 floor once instead of three times, so $4,000 more of her giving counts toward the deduction.

No tax was withheld from her 1099 income. She raises her December withholding to close the gap, which the IRS counts as paid evenly across all four quarters.

Nothing here is exotic. It’s the tax version of closing out your charts before a long weekend: routine work with a hard deadline.

Source: IRS Publication 505, IRS Publication 590-A, and IRC §404(a)(6). Chart: Doc Wealth.

Yes, but only on the employer side. The $24,500 employee deferral limit is shared across all your plans, so the Solo 401(k) takes an employer contribution of roughly 20% of your net self employment earnings.

It applies if you’re 50 or older and your 2025 FICA wages from the employer sponsoring the plan topped $150,000. Self employment income isn’t FICA wages, so catch ups to a Solo 401(k) funded only by 1099 earnings aren’t affected.

It depends on your MAGI. Below $505,000, itemizers can deduct up to $40,400 of state and local taxes. Between $505,000 and about $606,000 the cap shrinks, and above that it’s back to $10,000.

If your practice is in a state with a PTET, that election can still move state tax to the entity level.

You don’t necessarily need tons of money to do the things that make you happy. You can enjoy life now. Money can offer comfort and convenience. But you don’t need a certain amount of money to enjoy your life.

Identifying a check-in number is one of the easiest ways to improve how you manage money together, because it accomplishes two things that might otherwise seem at odds: preserving each partner’s financial autonomy while respecting your shared financial interests.

Many of us, when we identify a money problem and try to fix it, choose a solution that matches how bad we feel about the problem. Often, this level of solution is big enough to overwhelm us. Then the part of us that handles being overwhelmed takes over and does what it knows how to do — which is return to the old behavior.

There is some combination of sleep, diet, and exercise that is likely optimal, but optimal for whom? Every person is different, and that changes the equation. Similarly, there is some combination of growing, protecting, living, and giving that will be optimal for each person, each family, but you’ll rarely see an identical financial plan.

One of the most common questions around saving for retirement is: Am I on track? While it’s a good question to ask, there are a lot of factors that influence the answer. Between your future spending, your age, your family situation, and your financial goals, knowing whether you’re saving enough is harder than it looks. But what if there was a better way?
